conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: Describe the typical appearance of Bowen's disease.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: A well-demarcated, red, scaly or crusted PLAQUE — flat, solitary, and slowly enlarging over months to years. Often mistaken for eczema or psoriasis but is persistent and does not respond to topical steroids.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: Where does Bowen's disease characteristically occur?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: Sun-exposed skin, classically the lower legs of older women, but also head/neck. HPV-associated Bowen's can affect genital skin.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: What clue distinguishes Bowen's disease from eczema or psoriasis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: Bowen's is persistent, solitary, well-demarcated and does NOT respond to topical steroids — unlike eczema/psoriasis, which are usually multiple/symmetrical and steroid-responsive. A non-resolving 'eczema' plaque should prompt biopsy.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: Within an actinic keratosis or Bowen's plaque, which features suggest progression to invasive SCC?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: A new NODULE, induration, ulceration, tenderness, or bleeding within the lesion. Any of these should raise suspicion of invasive SCC and prompt biopsy.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: How is a small number of discrete actinic keratoses managed?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: Lesion-directed treatment: cryotherapy, curettage and cautery, or excision.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: How are multiple actinic keratoses or field change managed?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: Field-directed topical therapy: 5-fluorouracil (Efudix), imiquimod, diclofenac gel, tirbanibulin, or photodynamic therapy (PDT).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: What is the role of emollients and sun protection in mild actinic keratosis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: For mild disease, emollients plus strict sun protection and observation may be sufficient — treatment is not always required. Sun protection also reduces the development of new lesions.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: What is the first step in managing a suspected Bowen's disease lesion?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: BIOPSY — to confirm the diagnosis and exclude invasion (invasive SCC).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: List the treatment options for Bowen's disease.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: Topical 5-FU or imiquimod, cryotherapy, photodynamic therapy (PDT), curettage, or excision — after biopsy confirmation.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: Why are PDT or topical agents preferred over surgery/cryotherapy for Bowen's disease on the lower leg?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: The lower leg heals poorly, so PDT and topical treatments are favoured over surgery or cryotherapy to avoid chronic, slow-healing wounds/ulceration. Observation is also reasonable for small/stable lesions in the frail elderly.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: What is the referral pathway for actinic keratosis and Bowen's disease?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: Usually primary care management or ROUTINE dermatology referral — they are pre-invasive, so NOT 2-week-wait. A 2-week-wait referral is warranted only if invasive SCC is suspected.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: When should actinic keratosis or Bowen's disease trigger a 2-week-wait referral?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: When invasive SCC is suspected — i.e. a nodule, induration, ulceration, or rapid change developing within the lesion.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: What is a cutaneous horn and its significance?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: A conical keratotic projection that can arise on an actinic keratosis (or other lesions). Because an invasive SCC may underlie it, a cutaneous horn — especially if tender or indurated at the base — warrants biopsy.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: Summarise the AK → Bowen's → SCC spectrum.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: Actinic keratosis (partial-thickness, pre-malignant, scaly patch) → Bowen's disease (full-thickness, SCC in situ, red scaly plaque) → invasive SCC (keratotic nodule that can metastasise). Progression is signalled by a nodule/induration within a pre-existing lesion.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: Which patient population typically develops these lesions?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: Older, fair-skinned individuals (Fitzpatrick I–II) with cumulative sun exposure or immunosuppression. Chronic UV damage drives the whole spectrum.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: Why are actinic keratoses considered markers of 'field' cancerisation?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: They reflect widespread UV-induced dysplasia across a region of skin, so patients often have multiple lesions and an ongoing risk of new AKs and SCC — justifying field-directed treatment and surveillance.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: Does every actinic keratosis progress to SCC?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: No — the risk of progression per individual lesion is small, but because lesions are often multiple and reflect field damage, the cumulative population risk is significant, warranting treatment/surveillance.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: What is the histological hallmark separating Bowen's from invasive SCC?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: In Bowen's disease dysplastic keratinocytes involve the full thickness of the epidermis but the basement membrane is intact; in invasive SCC malignant cells have breached the basement membrane into the dermis.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: What is lentigo maligna?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: Melanoma IN SITU on chronically sun-damaged skin — atypical malignant melanocytes confined to the epidermis. It appears as a long-standing, very slowly growing, irregular pigmented patch, classically on the face of the elderly.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: What is lentigo maligna melanoma (LMM)?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: The INVASIVE form of lentigo maligna — malignant melanocytes have breached the basement membrane and invaded the dermis. Like any invasive melanoma it can metastasise and is staged by Breslow thickness.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: What is the melanocytic 'in situ' analogy for Bowen's disease?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: Lentigo maligna — it is the in-situ stage of a melanoma subtype (melanocytes confined to the epidermis), just as Bowen's disease is SCC in situ (keratinocyte dysplasia confined to the epidermis).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: Why does lentigo maligna (in situ) not metastasise?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: Because the malignant melanocytes are confined to the epidermis and have not breached the basement membrane. Metastatic potential appears only once it invades the dermis (lentigo maligna melanoma).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: Describe the typical appearance of lentigo maligna.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: A flat, irregular, variably-pigmented (tan/brown/black) macule or patch with ill-defined, asymmetric borders, enlarging slowly over years. It is often large by the time of presentation.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: Where does lentigo maligna characteristically occur?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: On chronically sun-damaged skin of the face — cheek, temple, nose — in elderly patients.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: How does the growth rate of lentigo maligna compare to other melanomas?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: It grows VERY slowly, over years, as an indolent radial in-situ proliferation — much slower than nodular melanoma. It shows ABCDE features but evolves very slowly.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: What clinical change within a lentigo maligna signals progression to invasive lentigo maligna melanoma?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: A NODULE, thickening, or focal darkening developing within the flat pigmented patch — indicating invasion into the dermis. This area should be biopsied.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: Why is Breslow thickness not applicable to lentigo maligna but is to lentigo maligna melanoma?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: Breslow thickness measures depth of dermal invasion. Lentigo maligna is in situ (epidermis only), so there is nothing to measure; once it becomes invasive (LMM) Breslow applies and determines prognosis and management.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: What investigations are used for suspected lentigo maligna?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: Dermoscopy (to distinguish from benign solar lentigo/seborrhoeic keratosis) and biopsy — sampling the most atypical/thickest area to detect any invasion.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: From which benign/pre-malignant lesions must lentigo maligna be distinguished?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: Solar lentigo, seborrhoeic keratosis, and pigmented actinic keratosis — dermoscopy and biopsy help make the distinction.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: Why should biopsy of a lentigo maligna target the thickest or most atypical area?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: To detect any focus of dermal invasion (lentigo maligna melanoma), which changes staging and management. A biopsy of a bland area could miss invasion.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: What is the first-line treatment for lentigo maligna (in situ)?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: Complete surgical excision with a clinical margin of ≥0.5 cm (as for melanoma in situ / stage 0).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: Why are Mohs or staged ('slow Mohs') excision often used for facial lentigo maligna?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: Because lesions are frequently large and ill-defined on cosmetically/functionally important facial sites, Mohs or staged excision allows margin control while sparing tissue — balancing cure against cosmesis.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: What non-surgical options exist for lentigo maligna when surgery is unsuitable?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: Radiotherapy, or off-label topical imiquimod; observation may be appropriate in the very frail elderly.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: How is invasive lentigo maligna melanoma managed?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: As for any invasive melanoma — wide local excision with margins guided by Breslow thickness (in situ ≥0.5 cm / stage I ≥1 cm / stage II 2 cm), ± sentinel lymph node biopsy if Breslow >1 mm.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: What is the referral pathway for suspected lentigo maligna or lentigo maligna melanoma?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: 2-week-wait (urgent suspected cancer) dermatology referral — it is a melanoma, so even in situ disease warrants urgent referral.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: Why is lentigo maligna referred under the 2-week-wait pathway despite being in situ, unlike actinic keratosis/Bowen's which are routine?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: Because it is a melanoma (a melanocytic malignancy with potential to progress to metastatic disease), so it is treated with the urgency of melanoma. AK/Bowen's are keratinocyte pre-malignancies managed routinely.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: What ongoing measures accompany treatment of lentigo maligna?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: Strict sun protection and skin surveillance, given the field of chronic UV damage and risk of further lesions.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: Summarise the in situ vs invasive fork for lentigo maligna.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: Lentigo maligna = melanoma in situ (epidermis only, flat macule, does not metastasise, excise ≥0.5 cm). A nodule/thickening within it = lentigo maligna melanoma (dermal invasion, metastasises, Breslow-guided WLE ± SLNB).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Seborrhoeic Ker.front: What is a seborrhoeic keratosis (basal cell papilloma, 'senile wart')?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Seborrhoeic Ker.back: An extremely common, BENIGN epidermal skin growth — pigmented papules with a waxy, 'stuck-on' appearance and keratin cysts — harmless, with no need to treat.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Seborrhoeic Ker.front: What is the 'core concept' of seborrhoeic keratosis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Seborrhoeic Ker.back: A benign overgrowth of the epidermis (keratinocytes) — its whole importance is recognising it as harmless and distinguishing it from melanoma (its pigmented mimic).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Seborrhoeic Ker.front: What two hallmarks flow from a seborrhoeic keratosis sitting ON TOP of the skin?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Seborrhoeic Ker.back: A 'stuck-on', waxy/warty appearance (as if it could be flicked off), and keratin cysts (horn cysts/plugs) on the surface and dermoscopy.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Seborrhoeic Ker.front: Who gets seborrhoeic keratoses, and where?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Seborrhoeic Ker.back: Very common; they increase with age (normal ageing skin), are often multiple, and occur on the trunk, face and back (not palms/soles).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Seborrhoeic Ker.front: What are the reassuring (benign) features of a seborrhoeic keratosis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Seborrhoeic Ker.back: A 'stuck-on', waxy/warty surface, keratin (horn) cysts, a well-demarcated border, uniform colour (tan → brown → black), and a stable lesion.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Seborrhoeic Ker.front: What features of a pigmented lesion should prompt exclusion of melanoma?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Seborrhoeic Ker.back: An irregular/evolving surface, no keratin cysts, an irregular/asymmetric border, variable/irregular colours, and change (growing, bleeding, ulcerating).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Seborrhoeic Ker.front: What does dermoscopy show in a seborrhoeic keratosis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Seborrhoeic Ker.back: Reassuring 'milia-like cysts' (white keratin cysts) and 'comedo-like openings' (± moth-eaten borders) — highly benign features (vs pigment network/atypical vessels in melanoma).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Seborrhoeic Ker.front: Why can a heavily pigmented seborrhoeic keratosis be a diagnostic challenge?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Seborrhoeic Ker.back: It can mimic melanoma — but on dermoscopy it shows the reassuring milia-like cysts and comedo-like openings.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Seborrhoeic Ker.front: What is the appearance of a seborrhoeic keratosis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Seborrhoeic Ker.back: Well-demarcated, round/oval, raised papules/plaques with a greasy, warty, 'stuck-on' surface; tan to dark brown/black; often multiple; with keratin (horn) cysts and a friable, crumbly surface; may itch or catch on clothing.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Seborrhoeic Ker.front: Where do seborrhoeic keratoses NOT occur?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Seborrhoeic Ker.back: The palms and soles (they occur on the trunk, back, face and scalp).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Seborrhoeic Ker.front: What is the sign of Leser-Trélat?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Seborrhoeic Ker.back: The SUDDEN eruption of MULTIPLE seborrhoeic keratoses (a rapid increase in number/size, typically over <1 year) → a paraneoplastic sign of an internal malignancy.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Seborrhoeic Ker.front: Which malignancies are associated with the Leser-Trélat sign?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Seborrhoeic Ker.back: Classically GI adenocarcinoma (stomach/colon); also breast cancer and lymphoma.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Seborrhoeic Ker.front: What should a sudden crop of many new seborrhoeic keratoses prompt?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Seborrhoeic Ker.back: Urgent referral and consideration of an underlying malignancy (especially with weight loss, GI symptoms or malignant acanthosis nigricans).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Seborrhoeic Ker.front: How is a seborrhoeic keratosis diagnosed?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Seborrhoeic Ker.back: Clinically (the characteristic stuck-on waxy appearance + keratin cysts); dermoscopy confirms the benign features; biopsy only if there is diagnostic uncertainty (to exclude melanoma/other).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Seborrhoeic Ker.front: What is the mainstay of management for a seborrhoeic keratosis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Seborrhoeic Ker.back: Reassurance — it is benign and harmless, so no treatment is needed.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Seborrhoeic Ker.front: When is removal of a seborrhoeic keratosis indicated, and how?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Seborrhoeic Ker.back: Only if symptomatic (itchy, catching, inflamed), diagnostically uncertain, or for cosmesis — by cryotherapy, curettage + cautery, or shave excision.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Seborrhoeic Ker.front: What is the biological behaviour of a seborrhoeic keratosis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Seborrhoeic Ker.back: Completely benign and harmless (though pigmented ones must be distinguished from melanoma clinically/dermoscopically).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Seborrhoeic Ker.front: Summarise the management rule for seborrhoeic keratosis.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Seborrhoeic Ker.back: Reassure (benign, no treatment); remove only if symptomatic, diagnostically uncertain, or for cosmetic reasons (cryotherapy/curettage).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.front: What is rosacea?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.back: A chronic, relapsing inflammatory skin disease of the FACE — recurrent facial flushing, persistent central erythema, telangiectasia, papules + pustules, and phymatous (rhinophyma) changes; crucially, it has NO comedones (the key distinction from acne).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.front: What is the 'core concept' of rosacea?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.back: A chronic inflammatory + vascular disorder of the central face — abnormal vasodilation (flushing → persistent redness → telangiectasia) + inflammation (papules/pustules) ± tissue overgrowth (rhinophyma).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.front: What three-part framework organises rosacea?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.back: (1) Recognise it and separate it from acne (rosacea = flushing/erythema/telangiectasia + NO comedones); (2) identify the dominant feature/phenotype (treatment is feature-directed); and (3) don't miss ocular rosacea (common + sight-threatening).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.front: Who typically gets rosacea?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.back: Common (~10%, underdiagnosed), age 30–50; women are more affected but MEN get rhinophyma; Celtic/fair skin and blue eyes are most at risk.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.front: What is the KEY feature distinguishing rosacea from acne?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.back: Rosacea has NO comedones (and has flushing/telangiectasia), whereas acne has comedones (blackheads/whiteheads) ± cysts.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.front: How does the distribution/age differ between rosacea and acne?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.back: Rosacea: central face (cheeks, nose, chin, forehead), age 30–50. Acne: face, chest and back, in adolescents/young adults.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.front: What are the differentials for rosacea?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.back: Seborrhoeic dermatitis (greasy scale, nasolabial folds), perioral dermatitis (around the mouth, often topical-steroid-induced), cutaneous lupus/SLE (photosensitive malar rash, no pustules), and systemic flushing causes (menopause, carcinoid, phaeochromocytoma).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.front: What are the features/phenotypes of rosacea?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.back: Flushing (recurrent transient, triggered) → persistent erythema + telangiectasia (erythematotelangiectatic) → papules + pustules (papulopustular, NO comedones) → rhinophyma (phymatous) → ocular involvement.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.front: What is rhinophyma?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.back: A thickened, enlarged, bulbous nose from sebaceous gland + connective tissue overgrowth — a late phymatous change of rosacea, mainly in MEN.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.front: Why is ocular rosacea a 'don't miss'?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.back: Ocular involvement is common (may precede skin disease) — dry, gritty, red eyes, blepharitis, conjunctivitis, styes/chalazia, lid-margin telangiectasia — and eye pain, photophobia or visual change signals keratitis (sight-threatening) → urgent ophthalmology.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.front: What ocular red flags in rosacea warrant urgent ophthalmology?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.back: Eye pain, photophobia or visual change (risk of keratitis).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.front: What are the common triggers of rosacea?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.back: Heat, sun/UV, hot drinks, alcohol, spicy food, stress, exercise and extreme temperatures.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.front: What is the 'steroid trap' in rosacea?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.back: Topical corticosteroids WORSEN rosacea (steroid-induced rosacea/rebound) → avoid them; a common trap is treating the redness with steroids.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.front: What general measures apply to ALL rosacea patients?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.back: Avoid precipitating factors, daily sunscreen (SPF ≥30), gentle emollients/skincare, and avoid topical steroids.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.front: What is the first-line topical treatment for the papules/pustules of rosacea?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.back: Topical ivermectin (first-line), or topical metronidazole, or azelaic acid.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.front: How is moderate-severe papulopustular rosacea treated?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.back: Add an oral tetracycline (doxycycline/lymecycline) at an ANTI-INFLAMMATORY (not antibacterial) dose.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.front: How do oral tetracyclines work in rosacea, and which are gentler on the stomach?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.back: They act as anti-inflammatory agents (not antibacterials); doxycycline and lymecycline cause less gastric irritation than tetracycline/oxytetracycline.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.front: How is the persistent erythema of rosacea treated?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.back: Topical brimonidine (or oxymetazoline) — an α-agonist vasoconstrictor.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.front: How is the flushing component of rosacea managed?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.back: Trigger avoidance ± (off-label) β-blockers/α-agonists (specialist).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.front: How are telangiectasia and rhinophyma treated in rosacea?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.back: Telangiectasia → vascular laser/IPL (specialist); rhinophyma → surgery/laser (specialist referral).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.front: What is used for refractory papulopustular rosacea?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.back: Low-dose oral isotretinoin (specialist).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.front: How is ocular rosacea managed?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.back: Lid hygiene, ocular lubricants, ± oral tetracycline; ophthalmology if red flags.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.front: What is the expected treatment timescale and review point in rosacea?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.back: Review at ~6 weeks, but expect to need at LEAST 3 months — rosacea responds slowly.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.front: When should rosacea be referred?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.back: For psychological/social distress; papulopustular disease not responding to 12 weeks of oral + topical treatment; rhinophyma; diagnostic uncertainty; or ocular red flags → ophthalmology.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.front: What is psoriasis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.back: A chronic, immune-mediated, inflammatory skin disease (a family of related diseases) characterised by well-demarcated, salmon-pink plaques with SILVERY scale, driven by accelerated keratinocyte turnover; chronic plaque psoriasis accounts for >90%.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.front: What is the 'core concept' of psoriasis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.back: T-cell inflammation → keratinocyte hyperproliferation — the epidermis turns over in days instead of weeks, so cells are shed before maturing → the thick, scaly, well-demarcated plaque.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.front: What three ideas organise psoriasis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.back: (1) The morphology (salmon-pink plaques + silvery scale on extensor surfaces + scalp, with the Auspitz/Koebner/nail signs); (2) it is systemic → psoriatic arthritis + metabolic/cardiovascular disease + psychological impact; and (3) a clear guideline treatment ladder.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.front: What is the typical onset and genetics of psoriasis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.back: Bimodal onset (late teens + 60–70s); a strong genetic component (~30% family history); commoner in Scandinavian populations.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.front: What are the features of chronic PLAQUE psoriasis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.back: Well-demarcated, salmon-pink plaques with silvery scale, symmetrical, on extensor surfaces + scalp (>90% of psoriasis).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.front: What is GUTTATE psoriasis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.back: Small 'raindrop' papules in children/young adults after a streptococcal throat infection; it may self-resolve.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.front: What is FLEXURAL (inverse) psoriasis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.back: Smooth, shiny, non-scaly red plaques in skin folds (axillae/groin) — the scale is rubbed off.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.front: What is PUSTULAR psoriasis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.back: Sterile pustules — localised (palmoplantar) or generalised (a dermatological emergency).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.front: What is ERYTHRODERMIC psoriasis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.back: Psoriasis affecting >90% BSA — a dermatological emergency (skin failure).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.front: Which types of psoriasis are dermatological EMERGENCIES?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.back: Generalised pustular psoriasis and erythrodermic psoriasis (skin failure).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.front: What are the triggers of psoriasis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.back: Genetics, streptococcal infection (→ guttate), stress, and drugs (Lithium, Beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors, Antimalarials/chloroquine, NSAIDs); sunlight usually relieves it (rarely exacerbates).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.front: What is the KEY safety point about systemic steroids in psoriasis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.back: Systemic steroid WITHDRAWAL can precipitate a pustular/erythrodermic flare → avoid systemic corticosteroids in psoriasis.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.front: What are the three classic signs of psoriasis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.back: The Auspitz sign (vigorous scraping of scale → pinpoint bleeding), the Koebner phenomenon (new lesions at sites of trauma), and nail signs (pitting, onycholysis, subungual hyperkeratosis).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.front: What is the Auspitz sign?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.back: Vigorous scraping of the scale produces pinpoint bleeding (from the thin suprapapillary epidermis over dilated capillaries); gentle scraping accentuates the scale.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.front: What are the nail signs of psoriasis, and their significance?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.back: Pitting, onycholysis, subungual hyperkeratosis (± an 'oil-drop' sign) — a clue to (and predictor of) psoriatic arthritis.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.front: What is the Koebner phenomenon in psoriasis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.back: New lesions developing at sites of skin injury/trauma (shared with lichen planus and vitiligo).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.front: Why must you always ask about joints in psoriasis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.back: Psoriatic arthritis occurs in a significant minority — ask everyone about joint pain/swelling and screen (e.g. the PEST questionnaire); patterns include DIP involvement, dactylitis, enthesitis and spondyloarthritis.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.front: What comorbidities are associated with psoriasis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.back: Cardiovascular disease + metabolic syndrome (obesity, diabetes, dyslipidaemia), IBD, uveitis and depression → assess cardiovascular risk and mental health.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.front: What general measures apply to ALL psoriasis patients?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.back: Emollients + lifestyle advice (stop smoking, reduce alcohol); explain the diagnosis, address psychological impact, and assess cardiovascular risk.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.front: What is the NICE first-line topical treatment for trunk/limb plaque psoriasis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.back: A potent topical corticosteroid ONCE daily + a vitamin D analogue (calcipotriol) ONCE daily — applied SEPARATELY (one morning, one evening) — for up to 4 weeks.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.front: What is the next step if trunk/limb psoriasis is not controlled after ~8 weeks of first-line topicals?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.back: A vitamin D analogue alone TWICE daily; then (8–12 weeks) a potent steroid twice daily (up to 4 weeks) OR coal tar; or a combined calcipotriol + betamethasone product (once daily — improves adherence).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.front: How is FLEXURAL/facial psoriasis treated topically?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.back: A mild-moderate topical steroid ± a calcineurin inhibitor (thin skin → short courses).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.front: How is SCALP psoriasis treated?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.back: A potent topical steroid once daily (up to 4 weeks) → then a combined calcipotriol/betamethasone gel.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.front: What topical add-ons help thick plaques in psoriasis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.back: Coal tar; salicylic acid/urea (descaling); and dithranol (short-contact).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.front: What is the safety guidance for topical steroids in psoriasis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.back: Short-term use (max ~4 weeks) to gain control; risk of local atrophy (± systemic effects if extensive); with annual review of steroid use.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.front: What phototherapy is used in psoriasis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.back: Narrowband UVB (extensive disease); PUVA (psoralen + UVA); guttate psoriasis → UVB.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.front: What systemic agents are used for severe/refractory psoriasis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.back: Methotrexate, ciclosporin and acitretin (methotrexate also for psoriatic arthritis).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.front: What biologics are used for severe psoriasis failing/unsuitable for systemics?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.back: Anti-TNF (adalimumab, infliximab, etanercept); anti-IL-17 (secukinumab); anti-IL-23 (guselkumab); anti-IL-12/23 (ustekinumab).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.front: How is guttate psoriasis specifically managed?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.back: Narrowband UVB + antibiotics if there is a proven streptococcal infection (it may also self-resolve).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.front: What is lichen planus?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.back: A chronic, immune-mediated (T-cell) inflammatory condition affecting the skin, mucous membranes, nails and hair — classically remembered by the P's and Wickham's striae; onset age 20–50, usually self-resolving.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.front: What is the 'core concept' of lichen planus?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.back: A T-cell attack on the basal keratinocytes (a 'lichenoid' interface reaction) → an intensely itchy, violaceous, flat-topped papular rash.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.front: What are the 'P's' of lichen planus?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.back: Purple (violaceous), Pruritic (often intensely itchy), Polygonal (angular-edged), Planar (flat-topped) Papules/Plaques.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.front: What are Wickham's striae?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.back: Fine WHITE lace-like lines on the surface of the papules (and oral lesions) — a near-pathognomonic sign of lichen planus.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.front: Where are cutaneous lichen planus lesions distributed?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.back: Flexor wrists/forearms, ankles/shins and the lower back; often symmetrical, with a Koebner phenomenon (lesions at trauma sites — shared with psoriasis and vitiligo).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.front: Why is it important to 'check other sites' in lichen planus?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.back: It is a multi-site disease — always check the mouth (lacy white striae), genitals, nails (pterygium) and scalp (scarring alopecia).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.front: What are the ORAL features of lichen planus?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.back: Lacy white reticular Wickham's striae on the buccal mucosa (asymptomatic and very common), or erosive oral disease (painful erosions — with malignant potential).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.front: What are the NAIL features of lichen planus?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.back: Longitudinal ridging, thinning and pterygium (dorsal scarring).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.front: What is lichen planopilaris?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.back: Lichen planus of the scalp → scarring alopecia (permanent hair loss).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.front: What is the malignancy risk in lichen planus?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.back: Erosive oral and genital disease is a potentially malignant disorder — malignant (SCC) transformation in ~1% (oral) → monitor and biopsy non-healing areas.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.front: What is a lichenoid drug eruption, and which drugs cause it?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.back: A drug-induced form of lichen planus — widespread/atypical, with timing related to the drug (onset and resolution with it); culprits include thiazides/other diuretics, antimalarials, anticonvulsants, NSAIDs and penicillamine (± ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers, gold).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.front: What are the other variants of lichen planus?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.back: Annular, hypertrophic (thick, on the shins — very itchy), flexural, bullous, actinic, lichen planopilaris (scalp/scarring) and erosive (oral/genital).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.front: What infection is lichen planus associated with, and when should you screen?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.back: Hepatitis C (± B) — consider hepatitis screening, particularly in oral/widespread/atypical disease (also linked to autoimmune thyroid disease).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.front: What is the typical course of cutaneous lichen planus?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.back: Onset age 20–50; cutaneous disease is often self-limiting (resolves over ~1–2 years) but may leave post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation; oral/genital/scalp disease tends to be chronic.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.front: How is lichen planus diagnosed?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.back: Clinically (the P's + Wickham's striae); skin biopsy if uncertain.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.front: What does skin biopsy show in lichen planus?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.back: 'Saw-tooth' rete ridges, a band-like (lichenoid) dermal lymphocyte infiltrate, and basal degeneration.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.front: What is the Koebner phenomenon in lichen planus?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.back: New lesions developing at sites of skin trauma (shared with psoriasis and vitiligo).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.front: What is the first-line treatment for lichen planus?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.back: Potent topical corticosteroids (± topical calcineurin inhibitors, especially for oral/genital disease).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.front: What are the escalation treatments for widespread/severe lichen planus?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.back: Phototherapy (narrowband UVB/PUVA) for widespread disease, a short course of oral steroids for severe/acute flares, oral retinoids (acitretin), and immunosuppressants (azathioprine, methotrexate, mycophenolate mofetil) for severe/refractory disease.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.front: What general measures accompany lichen planus management?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.back: Stop any culprit drug; antihistamines/emollients for itch; good oral/genital care for mucosal disease; treat hepatitis C if present; and monitor erosive oral/genital disease for malignant change (SCC).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.front: Summarise the reflex for lichen planus.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.back: Itchy, violaceous, flat-topped papules (± white lacy oral lesions) in a 20–50-year-old = lichen planus → check all sites, review drugs, consider hepatitis.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.front: How many 'P's' is lichen planus commonly taught with?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.back: The 6 P's — Purple, Pruritic, Polygonal, Planar, Papules, Plaques.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.front: What are leg ulcers and pressure injuries broadly?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.back: Chronic wounds from vascular insufficiency or sustained pressure — accurate classification drives management.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.front: What is the organising principle for leg ulcers and pressure injury?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.back: Determine the cause — venous (commonest) vs arterial vs pressure; and always check the ABPI before compression.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.front: What is the critical safety rule before applying compression to a leg?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.back: Check the ABPI first — compression on an arterial ulcer causes ischaemia (limb-threatening).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.front: What are leg ulcers?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.back: Chronic breaks in the skin below the knee that fail to heal (>2 weeks); the commonest are venous (~70%) and arterial, plus neuropathic (diabetic) and mixed.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.front: What is the master decision in leg ulcers, and why?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.back: Venous vs arterial — compression (the cornerstone of venous ulcer healing) is DANGEROUS (limb-threatening ischaemia) in an arterial ulcer, so every leg ulcer needs an ABPI before compression to exclude significant arterial disease.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.front: What is the location, appearance and pain of a VENOUS ulcer?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.back: Location: the gaiter region (around the medial malleolus); appearance: shallow, irregular border, granulating, exudative; less painful (better on elevation).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.front: What is the location, appearance and pain of an ARTERIAL ulcer?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.back: Location: distal (toes, dorsum, lateral malleolus); appearance: deep, 'punched-out', pale/necrotic base; PAINFUL (worse on elevation, better hanging the leg down).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.front: What is the location, appearance and pain of a NEUROPATHIC ulcer?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.back: Location: pressure points (sole, metatarsal heads, heel); appearance: punched-out, surrounded by callus; PAINLESS.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.front: What surrounding skin signs and pulses/ABPI characterise venous vs arterial ulcers?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.back: Venous: haemosiderin, lipodermatosclerosis, varicose eczema, oedema; pulses present; ABPI >0.8. Arterial: shiny, hairless, cold, pale skin, absent pulses; ABPI <0.8.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.front: What is the critical safety point regarding compression and arterial ulcers?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.back: NEVER apply compression to an arterial (or significantly mixed) ulcer — it worsens ischaemia → tissue necrosis/limb loss; this is why ABPI is mandatory before compression.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.front: What is the pathophysiology of venous ulcers?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.back: Chronic venous hypertension (incompetent deep/superficial/perforator valves; ± DVT history, varicose veins, obesity, immobility) → capillary damage + inflammation → skin changes and ulceration.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.front: What are the venous skin changes and their meanings?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.back: Haemosiderin deposition (brown pigmentation from red-cell breakdown), lipodermatosclerosis (fibrosis/hardening of subcutaneous fat → 'inverted champagne bottle' leg), a gaiter-region ulcer (medial malleolus), plus varicose eczema, atrophie blanche and oedema.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.front: What is the KEY investigation before compression in a leg ulcer, and what else is done?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.back: ABPI (to exclude arterial disease); plus Doppler/duplex (venous incompetence), swab only if infected, and screen for diabetes.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.front: What are the ABPI thresholds and actions for compression (UK/SIGN)?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.back: 0.8–1.3 → full (multi-component) compression is safe (the cornerstone); 0.5–0.8 (mixed) → reduced compression only under specialist supervision + refer; <0.5 → compression contraindicated → urgent vascular referral; >1.3 → calcified/incompressible vessels (diabetes/renal), unreliable → refer.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.front: What is the cornerstone of venous ulcer management?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.back: Full (multi-component) compression (when ABPI 0.8–1.3) — it heals and reduces recurrence.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.front: What wound/skin care is used for venous ulcers (NICE NG152)?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.back: Simple non-adherent dressings chosen by exudate; cleanse with water/saline; emollients + treat varicose (stasis) eczema (mild topical steroid); avoid routine topical antibiotics/antiseptics — only if clinically infected.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.front: How is the underlying venous disease treated in venous ulcers?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.back: Leg elevation, exercise, weight loss, and referral for endovenous ablation (early intervention improves healing and reduces recurrence — the EVRA trial).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.front: When should a venous ulcer be referred to a specialist/vascular service?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.back: If persisting >2 weeks / non-healing at 12 weeks / diagnostic uncertainty / suspected arterial or mixed / recurrent or atypical (reassess ABPI at 12 weeks).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.front: What causes arterial ulcers, and what are the risk factors?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.back: Peripheral arterial disease (atherosclerosis) → ischaemia → ulceration; risk factors are smoking, diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia and age.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.front: What is the management of an arterial ulcer?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.back: NEVER compress; urgent vascular referral → revascularisation (angioplasty/stent or bypass, urgent if critical limb ischaemia); cardiovascular risk management (smoking cessation, statin, antiplatelet, BP + diabetes control, exercise); wound care + analgesia; treat infection.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.front: What do arterial ABPI values mean?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.back: <0.9 = peripheral arterial disease; <0.8 with an ulcer = arterial; <0.5 = critical ischaemia; >1.3–1.4 = calcified/incompressible (diabetes/CKD) → unreliable, use toe pressures/vascular review.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.front: How is a neuropathic (diabetic) ulcer managed?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.back: Diabetic foot MDT, pressure off-loading, glycaemic control, debridement and treat infection (the ulcers are painless, at pressure points, with surrounding callus and a warm, well-perfused foot unless mixed).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.front: How is a mixed arterial-venous ulcer (ABPI 0.5–0.8) managed?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.back: Reduced compression only under specialist supervision, treating both components.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.front: What is a Marjolin's ulcer, and when should you biopsy?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.back: A squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) arising in a chronic wound — biopsy any chronic/atypical non-healing ulcer (rolled/everted edge, abnormal granulation) to exclude it.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.front: What is used to prevent pressure ulcers?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.back: Repositioning and risk assessment (e.g. the Waterlow score).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.front: What is a pressure ulcer (pressure sore, 'bedsore', decubitus ulcer)?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.back: Localised damage to skin and/or underlying tissue, usually over a BONY PROMINENCE, from sustained PRESSURE (± shear) → ischaemia + tissue death; it is largely preventable — a key NHS patient-safety/quality marker.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.front: What is the 'core concept' of pressure ulcers?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.back: Prevention dominates — sustained pressure over a bony point occludes capillaries → ischaemia → necrosis; shear (skin dragged over deep tissue) + moisture/friction accelerate it; because the mechanism is mechanical and predictable, they are mostly avoidable.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.front: What are the four mechanical factors causing pressure ulcers?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.back: Pressure (capillary occlusion → ischaemia), shear (deep tissue distortion), friction and moisture — sustained over a bony prominence.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.front: Who is at risk of pressure ulcers?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.back: The immobile (biggest — bed/chair-bound, paralysis, sedation, surgery), those with reduced sensation (neuropathy, spinal injury, stroke), the poorly nourished/dehydrated, the elderly with thin/fragile skin, and those with poor perfusion (arterial disease, diabetes, heart failure, smoking); plus medical devices.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.front: What are the classic SITES of pressure ulcers?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.back: Sacrum, heels, ischial tuberosities, greater trochanters, occiput, elbows and malleoli (bony prominences ± device sites).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.front: How are pressure ulcers classified?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.back: By DEPTH of tissue damage (international NPUAP/EPUAP system); NICE/NHS uses 'category' (not 'grade').

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.front: What is a Category 1 pressure ulcer?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.back: NON-BLANCHABLE ERYTHEMA of intact skin (harder to detect in darker skin).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.front: What is a Category 2 pressure ulcer?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.back: Partial-thickness skin loss — epidermis ± dermis (a shallow ulcer/abrasion or blister).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.front: What is a Category 3 pressure ulcer?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.back: Full-thickness skin loss — subcutaneous FAT visible, but bone/tendon/muscle NOT exposed.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.front: What is a Category 4 pressure ulcer?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.back: Full-thickness tissue loss — exposed/palpable BONE, TENDON or MUSCLE.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.front: What is an 'unstageable' pressure ulcer?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.back: Full-thickness loss where the depth is obscured by slough or eschar.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.front: What is a deep tissue injury (pressure)?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.back: Intact/non-intact skin with a localised purple/maroon area or a blood blister.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.front: Why is Category 1 harder to detect in darker skin, and what should you assess?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.back: Non-blanchable erythema is harder to see, so also assess skin temperature, firmness/oedema and pain — not just colour.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.front: Should stable dry heel eschar be removed?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.back: No — stable, dry, intact eschar on the heel should NOT be removed (it acts as a natural biological cover).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.front: How are at-risk patients identified for pressure ulcers (NICE CG179)?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.back: Use a validated risk-assessment tool alongside clinical judgement (Waterlow, Braden, or Norton), and assess skin integrity within 6 hours of admission (and on any change).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.front: What is the SSKIN prevention bundle?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.back: Surface (pressure-redistributing surface — high-spec foam, dynamic for higher risk), Skin inspection + care, Keep moving (reposition regularly + document frequency), Incontinence/moisture (barrier products), and Nutrition/hydration; plus heel offloading and device checks.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.front: What must you NOT do to prevent pressure ulcers (NICE CG179)?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.back: Do NOT use skin massage/rubbing to prevent ulcers.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.front: What is the management principle for an established pressure ulcer?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.back: Offload the pressure + wound care appropriate to the category + optimise the whole patient; involve tissue viability — and continue ALL prevention (the ulcer won't heal under continued pressure).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.front: What wound care is used for a pressure ulcer?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.back: Dressings chosen to manage exudate and promote healing (hydrocolloid/foam/alginate); document surface area (± photography); debridement of slough/necrosis (autolytic/sharp) EXCEPT stable dry heel eschar; no routine systemic antibiotics — treat clinical infection only.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.front: When are systemic antibiotics indicated in a pressure ulcer?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.back: Only for clinical infection (spreading erythema, cellulitis, systemic upset, suspected osteomyelitis) — treat infection, not colonisation; no routine antibiotics.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.front: What whole-patient measures aid pressure ulcer healing?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.back: Optimise nutrition (protein/calories — dietitian), involve the tissue viability nurse, obtain surgical review (debridement/flap) for large/deep (Category 3–4) or non-healing ulcers, and document/report (patient-safety incident) ± safeguarding review.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.front: What are the complications of pressure ulcers?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.back: Local infection → cellulitis, osteomyelitis (deep ulcers over bone), abscess; sepsis; chronic non-healing; pain; rarely a Marjolin's ulcer (SCC in a chronic wound); and significant morbidity/mortality and cost.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.front: What should a deep pressure ulcer over bone raise suspicion of?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.back: Osteomyelitis.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: What are immunobullous disorders?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: Autoimmune blistering diseases in which autoantibodies target skin adhesion proteins — the level of the split determines the blister type and fragility.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: What is the organising principle for immunobullous disorders?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: Where the antibody attacks — pemphigus = intra-epidermal (desmoglein) → flaccid fragile blisters, positive Nikolsky, mucosa involved; bullous pemphigoid = sub-epidermal (hemidesmosome/BP180) → tense robust blisters, elderly; dermatitis herpetiformis = sub-epidermal IgA, itchy grouped vesicles, coeliac-associated.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: Summarise the level/antibody and features of the three immunobullous diseases.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: Pemphigus vulgaris: intra-epidermal, anti-desmoglein 3 → flaccid blisters, +Nikolsky, painful mucosal erosions, middle-aged. Bullous pemphigoid: sub-epidermal, anti-BP180/230 → tense itchy blisters, elderly, mucosa usually spared. Dermatitis herpetiformis: sub-epidermal IgA → intensely itchy grouped vesicles on extensors, coeliac-associated → gluten-free diet + dapsone.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: How are immunobullous disorders confirmed?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: Skin biopsy + direct immunofluorescence.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: What is bullous pemphigoid?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: An autoimmune blistering condition — the commonest autoimmune bullous disease — in which antibodies attack the DEEP anchoring proteins of the basement membrane → producing TENSE, sub-epidermal blisters in the elderly.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: What is the 'core concept' of bullous pemphigoid (where the split is)?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: Autoantibodies target the hemidesmosome proteins BP180 + BP230 that anchor the epidermis to the dermis at the basement membrane → the split is DEEP (sub-epidermal) → the full-thickness epidermis lifts off as an intact ROOF → tense, robust blisters.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: What does the deep, roof-intact split of bullous pemphigoid explain?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: Tense (not fragile) blisters, a NEGATIVE Nikolsky sign, and mucosa usually spared.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: How does bullous pemphigoid differ from pemphigus vulgaris?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: Pemphigoid = deeper (BP180/230, sub-epidermal) → TENSE blisters, Nikolsky NEGATIVE, mucosa SPARED, elderly (>60), less severe. Pemphigus = superficial (desmoglein, intra-epidermal) → FLACCID fragile blisters, Nikolsky POSITIVE, mucosal erosions, middle-aged, more dangerous.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: What is the memory hook for pemphigoid vs pemphigus?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: 'Pemphi-GOID = GOOD/tense (deep, roof intact); pemphi-GUS = GRoss/flaccid + mucosa (superficial)' — or 'the deeper the antibody, the tenser the blister'.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: What is the mechanism of bullous pemphigoid?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: Anti-BP180/BP230 antibodies bind hemidesmosomes → complement + inflammation → sub-epidermal split → tense blister.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: What are the associations of bullous pemphigoid?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: Age >60; neurological disease (stroke, dementia, Parkinson's disease); and uncommonly an underlying malignancy.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: Which drugs can trigger bullous pemphigoid?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: Gliptins (DPP-4 inhibitors — a diabetes drug) and PD-1 inhibitors (immunotherapy for metastatic melanoma) → review the drug history.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: What is the pre-bullous (prodromal) phase of bullous pemphigoid?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: Itchy, urticated/eczematous plaques that may precede the blisters by weeks.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: What do the blisters of bullous pemphigoid look like?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: Tense, round, robust blisters (clear/serous/haemorrhagic) on normal or erythematous skin; often very itchy; mucosa usually spared.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: Is the Nikolsky sign positive or negative in bullous pemphigoid, and why?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: NEGATIVE — the split is deep (sub-epidermal) with an intact epidermal roof, so lateral pressure doesn't shear the skin (contrast the positive Nikolsky of pemphigus).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: What is the key investigation in bullous pemphigoid, and what does it show?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: Skin biopsy (2 samples): histology (lesional) → a sub-epidermal blister with eosinophils; direct immunofluorescence (perilesional) → LINEAR IgG + C3 along the basement membrane (confirmatory).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: What blood tests support the diagnosis of bullous pemphigoid?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: Serum anti-BP180 + BP230 (ELISA); ± eosinophilia.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: What are the immunofluorescence patterns of the three immunobullous diseases?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: Bullous pemphigoid = LINEAR IgG/C3 at the basement membrane; pemphigus = INTERCELLULAR IgG ('chicken-wire'); dermatitis herpetiformis = GRANULAR IgA at the dermal papillae.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: What is the first-line/topical management of bullous pemphigoid?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: A super-potent topical steroid (e.g. clobetasol) — first-line, especially for localised disease (as effective and safer than oral steroids); plus skin care — non-adhesive dressings, potassium permanganate soaks for weeping skin, and deroofing/aspirating large tense blisters (leaving the roof as a dressing).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: What systemic treatment is used in bullous pemphigoid, and what did the BLISTER trial show?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: Doxycycline (tetracycline) vs oral steroid — the BLISTER trial supported doxycycline as a safer first-line systemic option for many; steroid-sparing agents (methotrexate, mycophenolate mofetil) and rituximab for refractory disease.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: What drug-related step should not be forgotten in bullous pemphigoid management?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: Review and stop a culprit drug (gliptins/PD-1 inhibitors).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: Which age group and severity characterise bullous pemphigoid?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: The elderly (>60); it is generally less severe than pemphigus vulgaris.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: What is pemphigus vulgaris?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: A serious autoimmune immunobullous disease — antibodies against desmoglein (the desmosome proteins holding epidermal cells together) → a SUPERFICIAL, intra-epidermal split → flaccid, fragile blisters + painful ORAL and cutaneous erosions.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: What is the 'core concept' of pemphigus vulgaris?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: The 'superficial, fragile, mucosal' mirror of pemphigoid — autoantibodies target desmoglein (desmosomal adhesion between keratinocytes) → epidermal cells lose adhesion (acantholysis) → an intra-epidermal split → a thin fragile roof → flaccid blisters that rupture almost immediately, leaving painful raw erosions.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: What are the two defining consequences of pemphigus vulgaris?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: (1) The MUCOSA is severely affected (mouth erosions often the first and most troublesome feature — desmoglein-3 is in mucosa); and (2) Nikolsky's sign is POSITIVE.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: How does pemphigus vulgaris differ from bullous pemphigoid?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: Pemphigus = superficial (anti-desmoglein 1+3, intra-epidermal/acantholysis) → FLACCID blisters/erosions, Nikolsky POSITIVE, painful mucosal involvement, middle-aged (40–60), dangerous. Pemphigoid = deep (BP180/230, sub-epidermal) → tense blisters, Nikolsky negative, mucosa spared, elderly, less severe.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: What is the mechanism of pemphigus vulgaris?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: IgG autoantibodies against desmoglein 1 + 3 (desmosomal cadherins gluing keratinocytes) → loss of cell–cell adhesion (acantholysis) → an intra-epidermal split → a flaccid blister/erosion.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: Why does pemphigus vulgaris cause prominent mucosal disease?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: Desmoglein-3 is expressed in the mucosa and deep epidermis, so anti-Dsg3 causes prominent mucosal disease (mouth erosions first); anti-Dsg1 adds skin involvement.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: What are the causes of pemphigus vulgaris?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: Mostly idiopathic; some drug-induced (penicillamine, ACE inhibitors); with an HLA predisposition.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: What is often the FIRST feature of pemphigus vulgaris?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: Painful, non-healing oral/mucosal erosions — which may precede the skin disease by months.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: What do the blisters and skin look like in pemphigus vulgaris?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: Flaccid, fragile, thin-roofed blisters that rupture easily → painful raw erosions with crusting.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: Is Nikolsky's sign positive or negative in pemphigus vulgaris?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: POSITIVE — lateral pressure shears off the epidermis (the superficial intra-epidermal split).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: Which other mucosae can be involved in pemphigus vulgaris?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: Conjunctival, nasal, oesophageal and genital erosions.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: How does the dominant symptom differ between pemphigus and pemphigoid?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: Pemphigus erosions are PAINFUL, whereas bullous pemphigoid is itchy.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: Why should pemphigus vulgaris be considered in chronic mouth ulceration?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: Oral erosions are often the first and only feature for months, so it should be considered in chronic, painful, non-healing mouth ulceration.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: What is the key investigation in pemphigus vulgaris, and its histology?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: Skin/mucosal biopsy (2 samples): histology → an intra-epidermal split with acantholysis (rounded, separated keratinocytes; a 'tombstone' basal layer).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: What does direct immunofluorescence show in pemphigus vulgaris?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: Intercellular IgG ('chicken-wire'/fishnet) throughout the epidermis.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: What blood test tracks disease activity in pemphigus vulgaris?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: Serum anti-desmoglein 1 + 3 (ELISA).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: Contrast the immunofluorescence patterns of the three immunobullous diseases.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: Pemphigus = intercellular IgG (chicken-wire); pemphigoid = linear IgG/C3 at the basement membrane; dermatitis herpetiformis = granular IgA at the dermal papillae.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: What is the management principle for pemphigus vulgaris?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: Aggressive immunosuppression (systemic corticosteroids + steroid-sparing agents/rituximab) + skin/mucosal care — a serious disease needing systemic treatment (topical treatment alone is insufficient).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: What is the mainstay systemic treatment of pemphigus vulgaris?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: Oral or IV corticosteroids (the backbone), with steroid-sparing agents (azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil) and rituximab (anti-CD20 B-cell depletion — increasingly first-line with steroids for moderate-severe disease).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: What supportive/skin-mucosal care is used in pemphigus vulgaris?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: Skin care, non-adhesive dressings, emollient/topical steroids (adjunctive), oral care for mouth erosions, managing fluid/nutrition (painful mouth → poor intake), treating secondary infection, and monitoring immunosuppression.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: Why was pemphigus vulgaris historically fatal, and what changed this?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: It was fatal before steroids (fluid loss/infection like a burn); aggressive immunosuppression (corticosteroids ± rituximab) transformed the prognosis.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: At what age does pemphigus vulgaris typically present?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: Middle age (40–60).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: What is dermatitis herpetiformis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: An intensely ITCHY, chronic, blistering skin disease — a blistering dermatosis associated with COELIAC disease, responding to a gluten-free diet; essentially 'coeliac disease of the skin'.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: What is the 'core concept' of dermatitis herpetiformis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: The cutaneous manifestation of gluten sensitivity — the same autoimmune process as coeliac, in the skin: IgA antibodies (anti-transglutaminase) deposit in the dermal papillae → neutrophilic inflammation → sub-epidermal blistering → grouped, intensely itchy vesicles on the extensor surfaces.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: What are the two defining features of dermatitis herpetiformis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: (1) It is gluten-driven → >90% have coeliac disease (often silent) → a reason to diagnose and treat coeliac (gluten-free diet is the cornerstone); and (2) it is ferociously itchy ('herpetiformis' = herpes-like grouped vesicles, NOT a herpes infection).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: What does 'herpetiformis' mean in dermatitis herpetiformis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: It refers to the herpes-LIKE grouped vesicles — it is NOT a herpes infection.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: Which HLA types are shared between dermatitis herpetiformis and coeliac disease?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: HLA-DQ2/DQ8.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: How is dermatitis herpetiformis distinguished from bullous pemphigoid and pemphigus vulgaris?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: DH: grouped tiny intensely itchy vesicles (often excoriated) on EXTENSOR surfaces, GRANULAR IgA at dermal papillae, coeliac-associated → gluten-free diet + dapsone. Bullous pemphigoid: tense blisters, linear IgG/C3, neurological/drug associations → steroids. Pemphigus vulgaris: flaccid blisters/erosions, intercellular IgG (chicken-wire) → immunosuppression.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: What is the mechanism of dermatitis herpetiformis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: Gluten sensitivity → IgA antibodies against transglutaminase → IgA deposits in the dermal papillae → neutrophil recruitment → sub-epidermal blistering.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: What is the coeliac link in dermatitis herpetiformis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: >90% of patients have coeliac disease (gluten-sensitive enteropathy), though the gut disease is often silent/subclinical — DH may be the only sign of coeliac, yet they still have the enteropathy and its risks (malabsorption, osteoporosis, lymphoma).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: What are the clinical features of dermatitis herpetiformis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: Intense itch/burning (often severe, may precede lesions); small grouped 'herpetiform' vesicles + urticarial papules, symmetrical on EXTENSOR surfaces (elbows, knees, buttocks, scalp, shoulders); often excoriated (intact blisters hard to find); GI coeliac symptoms often silent.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: Where are dermatitis herpetiformis lesions distributed?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: Symmetrically on the extensor surfaces — elbows, knees, buttocks, scalp and shoulders.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: Why are intact blisters often hard to find in dermatitis herpetiformis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: The intense itch leads to the vesicles being scratched away, leaving excoriations and crusts.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: What is the KEY diagnostic test in dermatitis herpetiformis, and what does it show?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: Skin biopsy with direct immunofluorescence of PERILESIONAL (uninvolved) skin → GRANULAR IgA in the dermal papillae (the diagnostic gold standard).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: What does histology show in dermatitis herpetiformis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: A sub-epidermal blister with neutrophil microabscesses in the dermal papillae.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: What coeliac work-up is done in dermatitis herpetiformis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: Anti-tTG/anti-endomysial IgA antibodies (coeliac serology), duodenal biopsy (villous atrophy), check IgA level (IgA deficiency in coeliac), and FBC/haematinics (iron/folate/B12).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: What is the immunofluorescence pattern comparison across the immunobullous diseases?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: Dermatitis herpetiformis = granular IgA at the dermal papillae; bullous pemphigoid = linear IgG/C3 at the basement membrane; pemphigus = intercellular IgG (chicken-wire).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: What is the cornerstone treatment for dermatitis herpetiformis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: A strict lifelong gluten-free diet — it clears the skin (slowly, over months) AND treats the coeliac enteropathy, reducing long-term risks (malabsorption, osteoporosis, lymphoma).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: What is the role of dapsone in dermatitis herpetiformis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: It dramatically and rapidly relieves the itch/rash (within days) while the gluten-free diet takes effect, and is tapered as the diet works.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: What must be checked before, and monitored during, dapsone treatment?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: Check G6PD first (haemolysis risk); monitor for haemolysis, methaemoglobinaemia and agranulocytosis.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: Who should co-manage dermatitis herpetiformis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: Gastroenterology and a dietitian (alongside dermatology).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.front: Summarise the management of dermatitis herpetiformis.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.back: Strict lifelong gluten-free diet (treats skin + coeliac) + dapsone (rapid symptom relief; check G6PD).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.front: What is the organising principle for hair & pigmentation disorders?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.back: The pattern — alopecia areata = patchy non-scarring loss (exclamation-mark hairs, autoimmune); androgenetic = patterned thinning; vitiligo = well-demarcated depigmented macules (autoimmune melanocyte loss).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.front: What should be checked in alopecia areata and vitiligo, and why?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.back: Thyroid function — because of their autoimmune associations.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.front: What should sudden DIFFUSE hair loss prompt you to consider?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.back: Telogen effluvium and iron/thyroid causes.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.front: What is the master question in alopecia, and why?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.back: Scarring vs non-scarring — it determines reversibility: in non-scarring alopecia the follicle is preserved (potentially reversible/treatable), whereas in scarring (cicatricial) alopecia the follicle is destroyed and replaced by scar (PERMANENT — urgent to recognise).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.front: Give examples of non-scarring and scarring alopecias.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.back: Non-scarring: alopecia areata, androgenetic alopecia, telogen effluvium, tinea, traction. Scarring/cicatricial: discoid lupus, lichen planopilaris, folliculitis decalvans.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.front: What scalp findings suggest SCARRING alopecia?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.back: Loss of follicular openings, scarring and inflammation (vs normal skin in non-scarring).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.front: What is the framework for classifying non-scarring alopecia by pattern?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.back: Patchy (alopecia areata) vs patterned (androgenetic) vs diffuse (telogen effluvium).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.front: What is alopecia areata?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.back: An autoimmune, non-scarring alopecia — a T-cell attack on the anagen (growing) hair bulb → hair falls out in discrete patches (the follicle is preserved → hair can regrow).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.front: What are the features of alopecia areata?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.back: Discrete, round/oval, smooth, non-scarring bald patches with normal scalp skin; 'exclamation-mark hairs'; and nail changes (pitting, ridging).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.front: What are 'exclamation-mark hairs', and what is their significance?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.back: Short broken hairs that taper towards the scalp (wider at the top) at the patch edge — pathognomonic of alopecia areata.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.front: What is the spectrum of extent in alopecia areata?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.back: Patchy → alopecia totalis (whole scalp) → alopecia universalis (whole body).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.front: What autoimmune conditions are associated with alopecia areata?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.back: Thyroid disease, vitiligo, type 1 diabetes, pernicious anaemia, Down syndrome and atopy.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.front: How is alopecia areata managed?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.back: It is often self-limiting (many patches regrow spontaneously → reassurance); topical/intralesional corticosteroids (first-line, localised); topical minoxidil; topical immunotherapy (diphencyprone) for extensive disease; and JAK inhibitors (e.g. baricitinib) for severe disease.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.front: What features predict a worse prognosis in alopecia areata?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.back: Extensive disease, early onset, nail involvement and atopy.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.front: What is androgenetic alopecia?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.back: The MOST COMMON alopecia, affecting men AND women — a combination of hormones (androgens) + genetics → a receding hairline + miniaturisation of hair follicles → fewer, thinner hairs (non-scarring).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.front: What is the mechanism of androgenetic alopecia?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.back: Androgens (dihydrotestosterone, DHT) act on genetically susceptible follicles → progressive follicle miniaturisation → each hair cycle produces a shorter, finer, less-pigmented hair → visible thinning (follicles miniaturise but persist).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.front: What is the pattern of androgenetic alopecia in men vs women?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.back: Men: a receding hairline (temporal/frontal) + vertex/crown thinning (Norwood-Hamilton scale). Women: diffuse thinning over the crown with a preserved frontal hairline ('Christmas tree' on the part; Ludwig scale).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.front: What should female-pattern hair loss prompt screening for?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.back: A hyperandrogenic state — screen for PCOS (irregular periods, hirsutism, acne; androgens, LH/FSH, ± pelvic USS).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.front: How is androgenetic alopecia treated?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.back: Topical minoxidil (first-line, both sexes — prolongs anagen, slows loss/promotes regrowth); finasteride (oral 5α-reductase inhibitor — men, blocks testosterone→DHT, teratogenic so avoid in women of childbearing potential); anti-androgens (spironolactone, COCP) in women (especially PCOS/hyperandrogenism); plus hair transplant, low-level laser and cosmetic camouflage.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.front: Why is finasteride avoided in women of childbearing potential?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.back: It is teratogenic.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.front: What is telogen effluvium?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.back: Diffuse, non-scarring shedding ~3 months AFTER a stressor (major illness, childbirth, surgery, severe stress, weight loss, thyroid disease, iron deficiency, drugs) — the stressor shifts many follicles synchronously into the telogen (shedding) phase; it is self-limiting once the trigger resolves.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.front: What test is positive in telogen effluvium?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.back: A positive hair pull test (>10% of gently pulled hairs come out).
