conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.front: What is the management of telogen effluvium?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.back: Treat the trigger — it is self-limiting once the trigger resolves.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.front: Summarise the alopecia diagnostic framework.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.back: Ask scarring (permanent — lupus/lichen planopilaris) vs non-scarring (treatable); then within non-scarring: patchy (alopecia areata) vs patterned (androgenetic) vs diffuse (telogen effluvium).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.front: What is vitiligo?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.back: An acquired, autoimmune DEPIGMENTING disorder — total loss of pigmentation due to loss of MELANOCYTES → smooth, white, well-demarcated patches.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.front: What is the 'core concept' of vitiligo?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.back: Autoimmune destruction of melanocytes (the pigment cells) → affected skin has no melanin → depigmented (chalk/milk-white) patches.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.front: What are the two key consequences of vitiligo being autoimmune and depigmenting?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.back: (1) It is strongly associated with other autoimmune disease (thyroid, pernicious anaemia, Addison's) → screen; and (2) the depigmented skin has no photoprotection → burns easily and contrast worsens with tanning → sun protection is central.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.front: What phenomenon does vitiligo show, and what does it mean?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.back: The Koebner phenomenon — new lesions at sites of skin trauma (shared with psoriasis and lichen planus).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.front: What is the genetic predisposition in vitiligo?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.back: HLA-DR4 (it is common, often in younger people).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.front: How is vitiligo distinguished from other white/pale patches?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.back: Vitiligo = complete DEPIGMENTATION (chalk-white, melanocytes gone). Mimics are HYPO-pigmentation: pityriasis versicolor (hypopigmented, scaly, trunk, Malassezia/fungal), pityriasis alba (ill-defined pale patches, children, mild scale, post-eczema), post-inflammatory hypopigmentation (follows eczema/psoriasis), and tuberous sclerosis ash-leaf macules (congenital, genetic).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.front: What does a Wood's lamp show in vitiligo, and why is it useful?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.back: Vitiligo patches show bright, sharply-demarcated fluorescence (accentuated depigmentation) → it confirms the diagnosis and defines the extent, especially in fair skin.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.front: What autoimmune conditions are associated with vitiligo (to screen for)?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.back: Thyroid disease (Hashimoto's/Graves'), pernicious anaemia, Addison's disease (also type 1 diabetes and alopecia areata — the polyglandular cluster).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.front: What is the appearance and distribution of vitiligo?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.back: Smooth, white, well-demarcated, often symmetrical patches, on the hands, perioral + periocular skin, feet, elbows and ankles.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.front: What is the difference between non-segmental and segmental vitiligo?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.back: Non-segmental = symmetrical, generalised (common); segmental = dermatomal, younger patients, more stable (less common).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.front: How is vitiligo diagnosed?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.back: Clinically — depigmented patches ± Wood's lamp.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.front: What investigations screen for associated autoimmune disease in vitiligo?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.back: TFTs + thyroid antibodies (thyroid), FBC/B12 (pernicious anaemia), morning cortisol/short Synacthen if suspected (Addison's), and glucose/HbA1c.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.front: What is the management principle for vitiligo?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.back: Sun protection + vitamin D + psychological/cosmetic support; topical steroids/tacrolimus + phototherapy to repigment; depigmentation/grafting for refractory disease; ruxolitinib emerging.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.front: What general/supportive measures are used in vitiligo?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.back: SPF 50 (protect depigmented skin), vitamin D, cosmetic camouflage and psychotherapy.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.front: What topical treatments repigment vitiligo?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.back: Topical steroids and topical tacrolimus (a calcineurin inhibitor — especially the face, no atrophy).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.front: What phototherapy is used for vitiligo?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.back: Narrowband UVB (TL01) or PUVA.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.front: What options exist for refractory/extensive vitiligo?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.back: Bleaching agents (monobenzone/monobenzyl ether of hydroquinone — to depigment the remaining skin in extensive disease), laser and cellular grafting.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.front: Which emerging topical treatment is approved for non-segmental vitiligo?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.back: Ruxolitinib cream (a topical JAK inhibitor).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.front: Why is sun protection central in vitiligo?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.back: The depigmented skin has no melanin/photoprotection, so it burns easily, and tanning of the surrounding skin worsens the contrast.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.front: Summarise the vitiligo management ladder.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.back: SPF 50 + vitamin D + camouflage/psychotherapy → topical steroids/tacrolimus + narrowband UVB (TL01)/PUVA → depigmentation (hydroquinone)/laser/grafting for refractory; ruxolitinib cream emerging.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.front: What are erythema reactions?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.back: Reactive erythematous eruptions — hypersensitivity patterns triggered by infection, drugs or systemic disease; the two classics are erythema multiforme and erythema nodosum.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.front: What is the organising principle for erythema reactions?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.back: The morphology + site — EM = target lesions (acral), usually HSV-triggered; EN = tender red nodules on the shins (a panniculitis) with many possible triggers.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.front: What is erythema multiforme?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.back: An acute, usually self-limiting, immune-mediated skin eruption characterised by TARGETOID ('target') lesions — most often triggered by an INFECTION (classically HSV), not usually a drug.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.front: What is the 'core concept' of erythema multiforme?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.back: A hypersensitivity reaction — the skin's stereotyped response to a trigger (most commonly HSV), producing the pathognomonic target lesion (a concentric three-ring lesion), classically on the hands and feet (acral, extensor).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.front: What are the two priorities in erythema multiforme?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.back: (1) Recognise the target lesions + acral distribution and identify the trigger (usually HSV, or Mycoplasma in children); and (2) distinguish it from SJS/TEN (the dangerous, drug-induced, mucosa-severe conditions it superficially resembles).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.front: What are the three zones of a TYPICAL target lesion?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.back: Centre: dusky/purpuric or blistered (epidermal damage); middle ring: pale, raised, oedematous; outer ring: erythematous (red).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.front: What does an atypical (2-ring) target lesion raise concern for?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.back: SJS/TEN.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.front: How is erythema multiforme distinguished from SJS/TEN?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.back: EM: typical 3-ring target lesions, acral, INFECTION-triggered (HSV), benign/self-limiting, no/minimal mucosal involvement. SJS/TEN: atypical (2-ring) targets → dusky macules/sheet detachment, truncal→widespread, DRUG-triggered, severe mucosal involvement (≥2 sites), life-threatening (now regarded as distinct entities).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.front: What is the commonest trigger of erythema multiforme?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.back: Herpes simplex virus (HSV) — by far the most common; recurrent EM is usually HSV-driven (EM often follows a cold sore by ~1–2 weeks).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.front: Which trigger of erythema multiforme is common in children?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.back: Mycoplasma pneumoniae (± a mucositis-prominent variant).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.front: Which drugs can (less commonly) trigger erythema multiforme?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.back: NSAIDs, sulfonamides, penicillins, anticonvulsants and allopurinol.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.front: What are the clinical features of erythema multiforme?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.back: Acute, symmetrical, ACRAL target lesions (hands, feet, extensor limbs, face) spreading centripetally, which may follow a cold sore/infection by 1–2 weeks; usually mild ± itch/burning and NOT systemically unwell (unlike SJS/TEN).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.front: What is the difference between EM minor and EM major?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.back: EM minor = skin only, no/minimal mucosal involvement, benign; EM major = skin + mucosal involvement (usually oral, milder than SJS).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.front: How is erythema multiforme diagnosed?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.back: Clinically (typical target lesions + acral distribution); identify the trigger — HSV (cold-sore history; PCR of a lesion), Mycoplasma (CXR/serology if respiratory symptoms); skin biopsy only if uncertain (to distinguish from SJS/TEN).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.front: What is the management principle for erythema multiforme?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.back: It is self-limiting → mostly supportive; treat the underlying trigger; suppress recurrent HSV-driven disease with antivirals.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.front: What supportive treatment is used in erythema multiforme, and what is the timescale?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.back: Symptomatic — antihistamines, topical steroids for itch, analgesia; it usually resolves in ~2–4 weeks without scarring.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.front: How is HSV-associated (especially recurrent) erythema multiforme managed?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.back: Aciclovir — antiviral SUPPRESSION prevents recurrent disease (aciclovir/valaciclovir long-term).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.front: How is Mycoplasma-associated erythema multiforme treated?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.back: A macrolide or tetracycline (treating the Mycoplasma).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.front: How is EM major (mucosal) managed?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.back: Mouth care, ophthalmology if the eyes are involved, ± systemic steroids (debated).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.front: How does the distribution of EM differ from SJS/TEN?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.back: EM is acral (hands/feet, extensor, face) and symmetrical; SJS/TEN is truncal → widespread.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.front: What is erythema nodosum?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.back: A hypersensitivity PANNICULITIS (inflammation of subcutaneous fat) producing tender, red, raised nodules classically on the SHINS — a REACTIVE cutaneous sign of an underlying trigger (drugs, infection, pregnancy, or idiopathic).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.front: What is the 'core concept' of erythema nodosum?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.back: It is a REACTION PATTERN, not a disease — a delayed hypersensitivity response of the subcutaneous fat to a systemic trigger; its value is as a visible clue to what's happening internally, so spotting the nodules should immediately ask WHAT triggered it?

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.front: What is the natural history of erythema nodosum lesions?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.back: They are benign and self-limiting — resolving over weeks like a deep bruise, without ulceration or scarring.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.front: Where does the clinical work lie in erythema nodosum?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.back: In the investigation for the trigger, not the skin (the lesions are self-limiting).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.front: What are the main causes of erythema nodosum to look for?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.back: Streptococcus (commonest identifiable — recent strep throat), sarcoidosis, inflammatory bowel disease, TB, drugs (sulfonamides/penicillins/COCP) and pregnancy; idiopathic in ~half.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.front: What is Löfgren's syndrome?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.back: Erythema nodosum + bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy + arthralgia + fever = an acute form of sarcoidosis (good prognosis) — a classic exam association.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.front: What is the pathophysiology of erythema nodosum?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.back: A delayed (type IV) hypersensitivity reaction in the subcutaneous fat (a septal panniculitis), triggered by the underlying cause.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.front: What do the nodules of erythema nodosum look like?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.back: Tender, red/violaceous, raised, poorly-demarcated nodules, typically 2–5 cm.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.front: Where are erythema nodosum nodules distributed?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.back: Bilaterally on the shins (pretibial, extensor lower legs).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.front: How do erythema nodosum lesions evolve, and importantly what do they NOT do?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.back: They evolve like a deep bruise — red → purple → yellow-green → fade — and do NOT ulcerate or scar.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.front: What systemic features accompany erythema nodosum?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.back: Often fever, malaise and arthralgia (reflecting the trigger).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.front: Who most commonly gets erythema nodosum?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.back: Young women (20s–30s).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.front: What is the commonest infective cause of erythema nodosum?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.back: Streptococcus (a recent strep throat).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.front: Which drugs can cause erythema nodosum?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.back: Sulfonamides, penicillins and the combined oral contraceptive pill (COCP).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.front: How is erythema nodosum diagnosed?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.back: Clinically — the investigations are aimed at finding the cause.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.front: Which investigations look for the cause of erythema nodosum?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.back: Throat swab + ASO titre (Streptococcus), CXR (sarcoidosis — bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy — and TB), FBC and ESR/CRP, ± ACE and calcium (sarcoid), a GI workup if IBD symptoms (faecal calprotectin, referral), a pregnancy test, a drug history, and rarely skin biopsy if atypical (confirms septal panniculitis).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.front: What does CXR look for in erythema nodosum?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.back: Sarcoidosis (bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy) and TB.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.front: What is the management principle for erythema nodosum?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.back: Treat the underlying cause; the nodules are self-limiting → supportive care.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.front: What supportive measures are used for erythema nodosum?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.back: Rest + leg elevation, NSAIDs and compression (the mainstay) — it resolves spontaneously over ~2–6 weeks.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.front: What treatments are used for persistent/severe erythema nodosum?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.back: Potassium iodide or a short course of systemic steroids (once infection/malignancy is excluded).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.front: What is atopic eczema (atopic dermatitis)?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.back: A chronic, relapsing, inflammatory, itchy red rash — the commonest inflammatory skin disease of childhood, part of the 'atopic march' (eczema → asthma → hay fever).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.front: What is the 'core concept' of atopic eczema?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.back: A defective skin BARRIER + immune dysregulation — a genetically impaired barrier (classically filaggrin mutations) lets water out (dry skin) and allergens/irritants/microbes in → a Th2-driven inflammatory + itch response → the itch–scratch cycle perpetuates barrier damage.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.front: What are the twin mainstays of eczema treatment, and why?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.back: Emollients (restore the barrier) + topical steroids (damp the inflammation) — the whole treatment flows from 'restore the barrier + damp the inflammation'.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.front: Which gene mutation is classically implicated in atopic eczema?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.back: Filaggrin mutations (impairing the skin barrier).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.front: What is the 'itch–scratch cycle' in eczema?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.back: Allergens/irritants penetrate the defective barrier → inflammation → itch → scratching → more barrier damage — perpetuating the disease.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.front: What are the aetiological factors/triggers in atopic eczema?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.back: Genetics (atopic parent — barrier/filaggrin), irritants/allergens (soaps, detergents), diet/food allergy (cow's milk protein allergy), inhaled allergens (dust mites, pollens, pet dander, moulds), and stress.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.front: What are the UK diagnostic criteria for atopic eczema?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.back: An ITCHY skin condition PLUS ≥3 of: involvement of the flexures; a history of atopy (personal/family — asthma, hay fever, eczema); persistent dry skin; onset typically before 2 years old; and visible flexural dermatitis.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.front: How does the distribution of eczema change with age?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.back: Infancy: face, scalp and EXTENSOR surfaces; children and adults: usually the FLEXURES.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.front: What are the features of ACUTE eczema?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.back: Poorly-demarcated redness, vesicles, crusting, scaling, cracking and swelling.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.front: What are the features of CHRONIC eczema?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.back: Lichenification (thickened skin from scratching), dryness, scaling, cracking/fissuring, and post-inflammatory hyper/hypopigmentation.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.front: What is the cardinal symptom of eczema?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.back: Itch — eczema is 'the itch that rashes'.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.front: What suggests secondary infection of eczema?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.back: Weeping, crusting, pustulation, or erythema of normal-looking skin (swab if there is no improvement with emollients + topical steroids).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.front: What is the bacterial superinfection of eczema, and its treatment?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.back: Staph aureus — golden crusting/impetiginisation → antibiotics (flucloxacillin).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.front: What is eczema herpeticum, and its treatment?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.back: HSV infection of eczematous skin → monomorphic vesicles → punched-out erosions + fever/unwell → aciclovir (a dermatological emergency).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.front: What are the other complications of eczema?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.back: Sleep disturbance, growth impact, psychosocial effects, and steroid atrophy (thin skin from overuse).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.front: What is the principle of emollient use in eczema?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.back: Use them ALL the time, even when clear, 3–8×/day — the foundation of treatment.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.front: Which emollients/formulations are preferred, and which are avoided in eczema?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.back: Ointments have fewer preservatives and suit dry skin; avoid aqueous cream as a leave-on, avoid preservative-containing emollients (E45) as leave-on, avoid contamination, and bath additives are not recommended.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.front: How are topical steroids used in eczema flares?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.back: Acute → a strong steroid short course (7–14 days); chronic → the lowest appropriate potency, applied thinly; step up if not improving — watching for steroid atrophy.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.front: What is the topical steroid potency ladder by site in eczema?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.back: Child face → hydrocortisone (mild); child body / adult face → Eumovate (moderate); adult body → Betnovate/Elocon (potent); palms + soles → Dermovate (very potent).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.front: What is the main benefit of topical calcineurin inhibitors in eczema?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.back: Tacrolimus (Protopic)/pimecrolimus (Elidel) do NOT cause skin atrophy → steroid-sparing (e.g. for the face or steroid-resistant situations).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.front: What are the secondary-care escalation options for severe eczema?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.back: Phototherapy (narrowband UVB, PUVA) and systemics (steroids, methotrexate, azathioprine, ciclosporin); ± biologics (dupilumab) for severe disease; plus treating infection.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.front: Which biologic is used for severe atopic eczema?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.back: Dupilumab.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.front: What is the overall management ladder for eczema?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.back: Emollients (constant) + topical steroids (flares, site-appropriate potency) → calcineurin inhibitors (steroid-sparing) → phototherapy/systemics (severe) → treat infection + triggers.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.front: What are the referral criteria for eczema?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.back: Diagnostic uncertainty; severe eczema; moderate-severe eczema only partially responding to maximal treatment; steroid atrophy/concerns about steroid or immunomodulator use; and possible contact allergic dermatitis or occupational issues.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.front: What is the 'atopic march'?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.back: The tendency for eczema to be followed by asthma and hay fever.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.front: What is the prognosis of atopic eczema?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic.back: It affects ~10% of children and is rarer in adults — most improve with age.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What are dermatological emergencies?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Skin presentations that are life- or limb-threatening and demand urgent recognition and treatment.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What is the organising principle for dermatological emergencies?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Recognise the emergency by trigger + sign — a drug reaction with skin detachment (SJS/TEN), rapidly spreading infection with pain out of proportion (necrotising fasciitis), whole-body erythema (erythroderma), superficial peeling in a child (SSSS), or monomorphic punched-out lesions on eczema (eczema herpeticum).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What is the clue and action for SJS/TEN?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Drug trigger, mucosal involvement + skin detachment (+ Nikolsky) → stop the drug; supportive care/burns unit (SJS <10%, TEN >30% BSA).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What is the clue and action for necrotising fasciitis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Pain out of proportion, rapid spread, systemic toxicity, crepitus → urgent surgical debridement + IV antibiotics.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What is the clue and action for erythroderma?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: >90% body-surface erythema with fluid/temperature loss → treat the cause (psoriasis, eczema, drugs, lymphoma) + supportive care.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What is the clue and action for staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS)?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: A young child with superficial, toxin-mediated peeling (+ Nikolsky) → IV anti-staphylococcal antibiotics.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What is the clue and action for eczema herpeticum?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: HSV on eczema — monomorphic punched-out erosions in an unwell patient → urgent aciclovir.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What supportive principle applies to any widespread skin failure?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Attend to fluid balance, temperature and secondary infection (and stop the culprit drug in SJS/TEN, managing as a burn).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What is SJS/TEN?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: A severe, life-threatening mucocutaneous reaction — a spectrum of epidermal necrosis + detachment with mucosal involvement, most often a DRUG reaction: dusky erythema → full-thickness necrosis + desquamation, with extensive ocular + oral involvement.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What is the 'core concept' of SJS/TEN?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: SJS and TEN are the SAME disease at different severities — a type IV hypersensitivity reaction (cytotoxic T-cell/keratinocyte apoptosis) in which the epidermis dies and sheds off the dermis in sheets, like a superficial burn.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What two things make SJS/TEN an emergency?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: (1) The SKIN FAILS as an organ → massive fluid/electrolyte loss, thermoregulatory failure and a huge portal for infection/sepsis (the leading cause of death); and (2) MUCOSAL involvement (eyes, mouth, GU, airway) → blindness, strictures, airway compromise.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What is the single most important action in SJS/TEN?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: STOP THE CULPRIT DRUG, then supportive care in an HDU/burns unit.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: How is the SJS–TEN spectrum classified by % BSA detached?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: SJS = <10% BSA detached; SJS/TEN overlap = 10–30%; TEN = >30% — the same disease graded by skin loss (more detachment = higher mortality).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What mucosal involvement defines SJS/TEN?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Severe mucosal involvement at ≥2 sites (ocular + oral) — a defining feature.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: How does erythema multiforme differ from SJS/TEN?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: EM: typical targetoid (3-ring) lesions, acral (hands/feet, extensor), usually INFECTION-triggered (HSV, Mycoplasma), mild/limited mucosa, benign/self-limiting. SJS/TEN: atypical targets → dusky erythema/blistering/sheet detachment, truncal→widespread, usually DRUG-triggered, severe mucosal involvement, life-threatening (now considered separate entities).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: Which drugs classically cause SJS/TEN?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Anticonvulsants (carbamazepine, lamotrigine, phenytoin, phenobarbital), sulfonamides (co-trimoxazole)/penicillins/cephalosporins, allopurinol, NSAIDs (oxicams) and nevirapine.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What is the typical onset of SJS/TEN after starting the culprit drug?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Typically 1–3 weeks after starting the drug (certain HLA types predispose, e.g. HLA-B*15:02 → carbamazepine SJS in some Asian populations).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What is the prodrome of SJS/TEN?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Fever + flu-like symptoms, which may precede the rash by days.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What is an early clue to SJS/TEN in the skin?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Skin PAIN and tenderness out of proportion (painful dusky-red macules/atypical targets that coalesce into blisters and sheets of detaching epidermis).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What mucosal features occur in SJS/TEN?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Extensive ocular + oral erosions (conjunctivitis → blindness; haemorrhagic oral/lip crusting), plus genital and airway involvement.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What is Nikolsky's sign, and is it positive in SJS/TEN?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Lateral pressure shears off the epidermis — it is POSITIVE in SJS/TEN.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: How is severity/prognosis assessed in SJS/TEN?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: % BSA detached (SJS vs TEN) and the SCORTEN score (a validated mortality score — age, HR, malignancy, BSA, urea, glucose, bicarbonate).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What does skin biopsy show in SJS/TEN, and why is it useful?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Full-thickness epidermal necrosis — distinguishing it from staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome, which is superficial.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: How is SJS/TEN distinguished from staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: SJS/TEN: drug-induced (type IV), FULL-thickness split (dermo-epidermal junction), mucosa INVOLVED, any age, high mortality. SSSS: Staph aureus exfoliative toxin, SUPERFICIAL split (upper epidermis), mucosa SPARED, infants/children, good prognosis with antibiotics (both Nikolsky positive).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What is the immediate management of SJS/TEN?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: STOP THE DRUG (early withdrawal improves survival; stop non-essential drugs too), transfer to HDU/burns unit (treat like a major burn), and give fluid + electrolyte resuscitation and analgesia.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What supportive burns-type care is used in SJS/TEN?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Emollients (50:50 white soft/liquid paraffin) 2-hourly to denuded skin, non-adherent dressings, treat infection (cultures + treat; avoid prophylactic antibiotics), temperature control, nutrition, and multi-specialty input (ophthalmology, gynaecology/urology, dermatology, ICU).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What is the role of corticosteroids/IVIG in SJS/TEN?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: There is no consensus (immunomodulation is debated; ciclosporin and etanercept are used in some centres).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: Why is ophthalmology involvement critical in SJS/TEN?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: To prevent ocular scarring/blindness from the severe conjunctival involvement.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What is necrotising fasciitis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: A rapidly progressive, life-threatening bacterial infection of the DEEP soft tissues — spreading along the fascial planes with necrosis of fascia + subcutaneous fat — a surgical EMERGENCY.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What is the 'core concept' (lethal mismatch) of necrotising fasciitis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: The surface looks far better than the disaster underneath — the infection tracks rapidly along the deep (avascular) fascia, thrombosing vessels to the overlying skin, so early the skin can look deceptively normal/mildly cellulitic while beneath it the tissue is dying and the patient is becoming septic.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What are the two hallmarks of necrotising fasciitis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: (1) Pain out of proportion (the earliest, most important clue); and (2) rapid systemic toxicity/sepsis.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What is the management sequence for necrotising fasciitis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Recognise early → resuscitate → broad-spectrum antibiotics → URGENT surgical debridement (antibiotics alone don't work — the dead, avascular tissue must be cut out). DELAY = DEATH.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: How is necrotising fasciitis diagnosed, and what must you NOT do?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: It is a clinical/surgical diagnosis — do NOT wait for imaging; the definitive diagnosis is at surgical exploration.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: How is necrotising fasciitis distinguished from cellulitis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Necrotising fasciitis: pain out of proportion (early) → later anaesthesia, rapid (hourly) spread, systemic toxicity/sepsis, dusky/grey/mottled skin with haemorrhagic bullae/necrosis/crepitus, 'woody' induration beyond the erythema, and failure to improve on IV antibiotics. Cellulitis: proportionate pain, spread over days, mild systemic upset, erythema/warmth, improves on IV antibiotics.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: Why does the affected area become NUMB later in necrotising fasciitis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: The cutaneous nerves die (nerve death → anaesthesia) as the infection destroys the tissue.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What is Type I necrotising fasciitis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Polymicrobial (the commonest) — mixed aerobes + anaerobes; in older, diabetic or immunocompromised patients; affecting the abdomen/perineum/post-surgical sites (includes Fournier's gangrene).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What is Type II necrotising fasciitis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Monomicrobial — Group A Streptococcus ± Staph aureus; in younger, previously healthy patients; on the limbs; after minor trauma; can cause toxic shock.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What is Type III necrotising fasciitis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Clostridium (gas gangrene) or Vibrio vulnificus (marine/shellfish exposure).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What is Fournier's gangrene?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Necrotising fasciitis of the perineum/genitals — typically Type I (polymicrobial) in diabetic/immunocompromised men.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What are the risk factors for necrotising fasciitis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Host: diabetes (the biggest), immunosuppression, malignancy, chronic kidney/liver disease, obesity, alcohol excess, IV drug use. Portal of entry: skin breaks (trauma, wounds, surgery, ulcers, insect bites, injection sites) — sometimes no obvious entry.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What are the EARLY (subtle) features of necrotising fasciitis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Severe pain out of proportion to the skin (the key early sign), fever/systemic upset, and erythema/swelling that may look like cellulitis.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What are the PROGRESSING/systemic features of necrotising fasciitis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Rapid spread; dusky, grey, mottled skin → haemorrhagic bullae → necrosis; crepitus; skin anaesthesia; 'dishwater-grey' foul discharge; and sepsis/septic shock (tachycardia, hypotension, confusion, multi-organ dysfunction).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What is found at surgical exploration in necrotising fasciitis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Grey, necrotic, non-bleeding fascia that separates easily on finger dissection — a 'positive finger test'.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What supporting blood tests are seen in necrotising fasciitis, and what is the LRINEC score's role?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Raised WCC/CRP, deranged U&E, high lactate and high CK; the LRINEC score supports suspicion but a LOW score does NOT exclude it (blood + tissue cultures guide antibiotics).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What is the role of imaging in necrotising fasciitis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: CT/MRI/X-ray may show gas in the tissues or fascial oedema — useful only if it doesn't delay surgery; a normal scan does NOT exclude it.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What is the management principle for necrotising fasciitis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Resuscitate + broad-spectrum antibiotics + URGENT surgical debridement (the definitive treatment) — all simultaneously and immediately.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What antibiotics are used in necrotising fasciitis, and why add clindamycin?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics immediately (aerobes + anaerobes + Gram-negative) — e.g. a carbapenem or piperacillin-tazobactam + clindamycin; clindamycin suppresses bacterial toxin/exotoxin (especially Group A Strep). Antibiotics alone are NOT sufficient.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What is the definitive treatment for necrotising fasciitis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Urgent radical debridement of ALL necrotic tissue back to healthy, bleeding tissue — often needing repeated ('second-look') debridements, with amputation if unsalvageable.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What is the strongest predictor of death in necrotising fasciitis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Delay to surgery — speed is everything.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What additional supportive measures are used in necrotising fasciitis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: ICU care; Fournier's/perineal → urology/surgery (± stoma) with later reconstruction; ± IVIG for streptococcal toxic shock; ± hyperbaric oxygen (unproven).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What is erythroderma (exfoliative dermatitis)?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Generalised redness + scaling affecting >90% of the body surface ('red all over') — a dermatological EMERGENCY (a reaction pattern, not a single disease).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What is the 'core concept' of erythroderma?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: It is a severe reaction pattern — the endpoint many skin diseases reach when they generalise; when >90% of the skin is inflamed, the SKIN FAILS as an organ (barrier, thermoregulation, fluid retention collapse), like extensive burns.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What are the two tasks in managing erythroderma?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: (1) Recognise + treat the systemic complications (emergency supportive care); and (2) identify + treat the underlying cause (which differs by cause, and one — cutaneous lymphoma — is a malignancy).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What are the causes of erythroderma?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Eczema (atopic dermatitis), psoriasis, drug eruptions, cutaneous lymphoma (cutaneous T-cell lymphoma/Sézary syndrome — the malignant cause), pityriasis rubra pilaris, and idiopathic.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: Which causes of erythroderma are commonest, and what must always be considered?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Pre-existing skin disease (eczema/psoriasis) is commonest; always exclude a drug and consider lymphoma.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What clues point to eczema as the cause of erythroderma?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Pre-existing eczema, a flexural pattern and itch.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What clues point to psoriasis as the cause of erythroderma?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Pre-existing plaques and nail changes; it may follow steroid withdrawal or other triggers.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What clues point to a drug cause of erythroderma?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: A recent new drug (1–3 weeks); ± DRESS (fever, eosinophilia, organ involvement).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: Which malignant cause of erythroderma should be considered, and how is it detected?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides/Sézary syndrome) — in an older patient with erythroderma + lymphadenopathy, look for Sézary cells on the blood film.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What clues point to pityriasis rubra pilaris as the cause of erythroderma?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Orange-red colour, 'islands of sparing', and palmoplantar keratoderma.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What are the skin features of erythroderma?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Widespread bright red, warm skin over >90% BSA with scaling/exfoliation, intense itch and a tight feeling; later thickening/lichenification.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What systemic complications result from skin failure in erythroderma?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Hypothermia (lost thermoregulation), fluid/electrolyte loss and dehydration, hypoalbuminaemia + oedema, high-output cardiac failure (cutaneous vasodilation), and infection/sepsis (the leading cause of death).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What is the leading cause of death in erythroderma?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Infection/sepsis.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: Why does erythroderma cause high-output cardiac failure?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Widespread cutaneous vasodilation increases cardiac demand.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What systemic investigations are done in erythroderma?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Assess the systemic effects — temperature, fluid balance, U&E, albumin, FBC, CRP, cultures (sepsis screen).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What investigations help find the cause of erythroderma?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Skin biopsy (may show psoriasis/eczema/lymphoma/pityriasis rubra pilaris), blood film (Sézary cells → cutaneous T-cell lymphoma), eosinophilia (drug/DRESS) and a careful drug history.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What is the management principle for erythroderma?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Admit — emergency supportive care (like a burn) + treat the underlying cause + STOP any culprit drug.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What supportive (emergency) measures are used in erythroderma?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Fluid + electrolyte replacement, warming (correct hypothermia), monitor/support cardiac function, nutrition, treat/prevent infection; and skin care with liberal emollients (the mainstay), wet wraps, mild topical steroids and non-adherent dressings.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: How is the underlying cause treated in erythroderma?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Stop any culprit drug; treat eczema/psoriasis flares (for psoriasis, avoid systemic steroids — rebound; use methotrexate/ciclosporin/biologics); cutaneous lymphoma (Sézary) → oncology/haematology; pityriasis rubra pilaris → retinoids/methotrexate.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: Why should systemic steroids be avoided in psoriatic erythroderma?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: They can cause rebound (worsening) — so methotrexate/ciclosporin/biologics are used instead.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What is staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS)?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: A superficial blistering condition of young children caused by exfoliative (epidermolytic) TOXINS released by Staphylococcus aureus → erythema + superficial desquamation with a positive Nikolsky's sign, so the skin looks scalded/burned.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What is the 'core concept' of SSSS (toxin-mediated)?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: It is toxin-mediated, not a direct skin infection — a Staph aureus infection (often at a distant, trivial site) releases exfoliative toxins A + B into the circulation, which cleave desmoglein-1 (holding upper epidermal cells together) → the superficial epidermis splits and peels in sheets, like a scald.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: Which molecule do the exfoliative toxins of SSSS cleave, and where?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Desmoglein-1 in the superficial (granular-layer) epidermis → loss of adhesion → superficial split → peeling.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: From where does the Staph aureus toxin originate in SSSS?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: A distant/trivial infective site — the nose, throat, umbilicus or conjunctiva (or skin) — releasing the toxin into the blood.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: Why does SSSS spare the mucous membranes?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: The split is superficial and the mucosa lacks desmoglein-1, so it is not affected.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: Why does SSSS affect young children/neonates?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Immature renal clearance of the toxin plus a lack of protective anti-toxin antibodies (rarely adults with renal failure/immunocompromise).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: How does the split in SSSS differ from that in TEN, and what does this mean for healing?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: SSSS = a SUPERFICIAL (upper epidermal) split → heals WITHOUT scarring and spares mucosa; TEN = a FULL-thickness (dermo-epidermal junction) split with mucosal involvement.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: How is SSSS distinguished from toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN)?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: SSSS: Staph toxin, infants/young children, superficial split, mucosa SPARED, good prognosis (antibiotics). TEN: drug reaction (type IV), any age/adults, full-thickness split, mucosa severely involved, high mortality (both Nikolsky positive).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What is the prodrome of SSSS?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Fever, irritability and malaise; ± the source infection (conjunctivitis, sore throat).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What are the skin features of SSSS?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Diffuse, tender, red skin (often starting periorally and in the flexures) → flaccid blisters → superficial peeling ('scalded'); a positive Nikolsky's sign; with characteristic perioral crusting and radial fissuring around the mouth, and skin pain/tenderness.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What is the characteristic facial feature of SSSS?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Perioral crusting with radial fissuring around the mouth.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: How is SSSS diagnosed?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Largely clinically (the characteristic picture in a young child); identify the source infection with swabs/cultures from the likely primary site (nose, throat, conjunctiva, umbilicus).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: Why is the blister fluid in SSSS usually sterile?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: It is toxin-mediated, not an infection of the skin itself — so the blister fluid is usually sterile (culture the source, not the blister).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What does skin biopsy show in SSSS?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: A superficial (subcorneal/granular-layer) split — as opposed to the full-thickness necrosis of TEN.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What is the definitive treatment of SSSS?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Anti-staphylococcal antibiotics — IV (e.g. flucloxacillin) to eradicate the Staph aureus source (± clindamycin to suppress toxin); it responds well (unlike TEN).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What supportive measures are used in SSSS?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Fluid + electrolyte management (barrier loss → fluid loss, like a superficial burn), analgesia, temperature control, and emollients/non-adherent dressings for denuded skin; avoid steroids.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What is the prognosis of SSSS?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Generally good in children — it heals WITHOUT scarring (superficial split) within ~1–2 weeks (worse in adults with comorbidity/renal failure).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: Summarise the SSSS exam picture.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: A febrile, unwell young child with diffuse tender erythema → superficial peeling/blistering + perioral crusting + positive Nikolsky's, with SPARED mucosa = SSSS → anti-staphylococcal antibiotics.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What is eczema herpeticum?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: A widespread, potentially life-threatening herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection of eczematous (or barrier-damaged) skin — a dermatological EMERGENCY: red, inflamed skin covered with raised scaly patches + small vesicles or pustules.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What is the 'core concept' of eczema herpeticum?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: What happens when HSV infects skin whose barrier is already broken by eczema — normally HSV causes a localised cold sore, but in atopic eczema the impaired barrier + local immune dysfunction let the virus spread widely and rapidly (a disseminated, monomorphic vesicular eruption).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What two things make eczema herpeticum an emergency?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: (1) Systemic dissemination (viraemia; rarely HSV encephalitis/hepatitis/keratitis); and (2) secondary bacterial superinfection + sepsis.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What is the single most important action in eczema herpeticum?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Early recognition → prompt aciclovir (don't wait for confirmation).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: How is eczema herpeticum distinguished from a bacterially infected eczema flare?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Eczema herpeticum (viral/HSV): MONOMORPHIC clustered vesicles → 'punched-out' uniform round erosions, with fever/systemic upset, rapid and widespread → aciclovir. Bacterially infected eczema (staph/strep): golden/honey crusting (impetigo), pustules, ± mild systemic upset → anti-staph antibiotics (flucloxacillin).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What is the classic 'punched-out' sign of eczema herpeticum?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Ruptured vesicles leave numerous small, uniform, round, crusted, 'punched-out' erosions.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: Why does eczema herpeticum often need BOTH aciclovir and antibiotics?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: It is frequently co-infected with bacteria (staph/strep), so it often needs both antiviral and antibacterial treatment.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What is the mechanism of eczema herpeticum?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: HSV (usually HSV-1) infects skin with a defective barrier and impaired local immunity — atopic eczema is the classic setting (barrier defect + Th2-skewed immunity allow spread); the source is a cold sore (own or a contact's).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What are the risk factors for eczema herpeticum?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Active/severe atopic eczema and other barrier-defective skin (Darier's disease, burns, pemphigus, cutaneous T-cell lymphoma); young children; immunosuppression.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What are the clinical features of eczema herpeticum?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Rapidly worsening, PAINFUL eczema; clusters of uniform, dome-shaped monomorphic vesicles/pustules on eczematous skin → punched-out erosions; systemic fever, malaise, lethargy and lymphadenopathy (the child is unwell); often on the face and neck but can be widespread.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: Why is pain a useful clue in eczema herpeticum?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: The affected skin is painful — a clue distinguishing it from the usually itchy eczema.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What are the red flags for dissemination in eczema herpeticum?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Eye involvement (HSV keratitis → ophthalmology emergency), signs of encephalitis, or sepsis.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: How is eczema herpeticum diagnosed?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Largely clinically — treat on suspicion and do NOT wait; start aciclovir empirically while confirming with a viral swab (from a vesicle) for HSV PCR (± a bacterial swab for co-infection).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What is the management principle for eczema herpeticum?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Prompt aciclovir (± IV if severe/systemic) + treat bacterial co-infection + supportive skin care + ophthalmology if eyes involved; do NOT delay.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: When is IV (vs oral) aciclovir used in eczema herpeticum?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: IV aciclovir if systemically unwell, extensive, immunocompromised, or a young child; oral aciclovir for mild/localised disease — started early.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: What adjunctive treatments are used in eczema herpeticum?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Anti-staph/strep antibiotics (flucloxacillin) for bacterial co-infection (common), analgesia, fluids, continuing emollients, and caution with topical steroids on actively infected skin; admit if systemically unwell/extensive/young/immunocompromised or with eye involvement.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: Why is urgent ophthalmology referral needed if the eyes are involved in eczema herpeticum?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: Periocular/eye involvement risks HSV keratitis, which threatens sight — an ophthalmology emergency.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.front: Which virus and setting are classic for eczema herpeticum?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Dermatological.back: HSV (usually HSV-1) in a child with active atopic eczema, from a cold sore source.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: What are cutaneous signs of systemic disease?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: Skin findings that are external clues to internal disease — metabolic, endocrine or malignant — recognising them prompts the systemic work-up.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: What is the organising principle for cutaneous signs of systemic disease?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: The skin sign points to the underlying disease — acanthosis nigricans → insulin resistance (or, if rapid, GI malignancy); necrobiosis lipoidica → diabetes; necrolytic migratory erythema → glucagonoma.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: What are the appearance and associations of the three key cutaneous signs?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: Acanthosis nigricans: velvety flexural/neck hyperpigmentation → insulin resistance/obesity/T2DM (rapid onset → GI adenocarcinoma). Necrobiosis lipoidica: yellow-brown shiny atrophic shin plaques → diabetes. Necrolytic migratory erythema: migratory erythematous erosive rash → glucagonoma (+ weight loss, diabetes).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: Why should a new/rapidly progressive skin sign prompt investigation?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: It can be the first presentation of internal disease — investigate for the associated condition (glucose, malignancy screen as appropriate).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: What is acanthosis nigricans?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: Symmetrical, velvety, hyperpigmented (brown-black) thickening of the skin, classically in the body folds/flexures (axillae, neck, groin) — a cutaneous SIGN of an underlying systemic process, most often insulin resistance.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: What is the 'core concept' of acanthosis nigricans?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: It is not a disease in itself but a SKIN MARKER; the dominant mechanism is insulin resistance — high circulating insulin cross-activates IGF-1 receptors on keratinocytes/fibroblasts → epidermal proliferation → the velvety thickening.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: What is the key response to spotting acanthosis nigricans?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: Think insulin resistance → screen for type 2 diabetes / obesity / PCOS.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: What is the crucial exception (malignant form) of acanthosis nigricans?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: A rare but dangerous paraneoplastic acanthosis nigricans (usually gastric adenocarcinoma) that appears suddenly, extensively and atypically in a non-obese adult → prompting a cancer search.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: How is benign (insulin-resistance) acanthosis nigricans distinguished from the malignant (paraneoplastic) form?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: Benign: gradual, flexural (neck/axillae/groin), obese/younger/darker-skinned, insulin resistance, usually no itch. Malignant: sudden + rapidly progressive, extensive/atypical (mucous membranes, lips, palms/'tripe palms'), older/often non-obese with weight loss, internal malignancy (esp. gastric), often itchy.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: What are 'tripe palms', and what do they suggest?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: Thickened, velvety, ridged palms — which, with sudden extensive acanthosis nigricans, strongly suggest an underlying malignancy.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: What are the causes of acanthosis nigricans?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: Insulin resistance (commonest — obesity, type 2 diabetes, metabolic syndrome, PCOS); endocrine (Cushing's, acromegaly, hypothyroidism); drugs (corticosteroids, nicotinic acid, the COCP, insulin); malignancy (paraneoplastic — gastric adenocarcinoma commonest, other GI/GU cancers); and rare genetic/familial forms.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: What is the PCOS link with acanthosis nigricans?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: Acanthosis nigricans + hirsutism + irregular periods + obesity = PCOS (insulin resistance) — a classic association.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: Where do acanthosis nigricans plaques appear?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: Symmetrical velvety plaques on the posterior/lateral neck (commonest), axillae, groin, antecubital/popliteal fossae and umbilicus; thickened and velvety, they don't wash off and are usually asymptomatic.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: What skin lesion commonly accompanies acanthosis nigricans, and why?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: Skin tags (acrochordons) in the same areas — both are insulin-resistance signs.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: How is acanthosis nigricans diagnosed?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: Clinically — the characteristic velvety flexural plaques; biopsy is rarely needed.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: What investigations assess insulin resistance in acanthosis nigricans?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: Fasting glucose, HbA1c, ± fasting insulin/lipids and BMI/weight; a PCOS work-up if relevant (androgens, LH/FSH, pelvic USS); and an endocrine screen (Cushing's/acromegaly/TFTs) if suggested.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: When is a malignancy screen indicated in acanthosis nigricans, and what does it involve?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: If sudden/extensive/atypical/non-obese ± weight loss — examination, endoscopy (gastric), imaging and tumour markers.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: What is the management principle for acanthosis nigricans?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: Treat the UNDERLYING CAUSE — the skin follows; there is no specific cure for the plaques themselves.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: How is the common (insulin-resistance) form of acanthosis nigricans managed?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: Weight loss + lifestyle + treat diabetes (metformin — improving insulin sensitivity often improves the skin); stop a causative drug; treat the endocrinopathy/PCOS.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: How is the malignant form of acanthosis nigricans managed?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: Treat the underlying cancer — the skin may regress with successful treatment.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: What skin-directed (cosmetic) options exist for acanthosis nigricans?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: Topical retinoids, keratolytics (urea, salicylic acid) and topical vitamin D analogues — the plaques are otherwise harmless.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: What is necrobiosis lipoidica?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: A chronic granulomatous skin condition producing well-demarcated, shiny, atrophic yellow-brown plaques, classically on the SHINS (pretibial) — strongly associated with diabetes (historically 'necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum').

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: What is the 'core concept' of necrobiosis lipoidica?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: Another cutaneous sign of systemic disease — its importance is the link with diabetes and its tendency to ulcerate; the pathology is degeneration of dermal collagen ('necrobiosis') + a granulomatous response → an atrophic waxy yellow plaque with visible telangiectasia.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: What two threads dominate necrobiosis lipoidica?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: (1) It should prompt thinking of/screening for diabetes (though not all patients are diabetic, and treating diabetes doesn't reliably improve the skin); and (2) the plaques are fragile and prone to ulceration.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: What does a necrobiosis lipoidica plaque look like?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: A shiny, atrophic, yellow-brown plaque with telangiectasia and a raised violaceous border, on the pretibial shins.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: Why can you 'see through' a necrobiosis lipoidica plaque?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: It is atrophic — the epidermis thins so you can see the underlying dermal vessels (telangiectasia) through the waxy yellow surface.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: What is the key systemic association of necrobiosis lipoidica?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: Diabetes mellitus (type 1 > type 2) — but only a minority of patients are diabetic at presentation, and it affects only a small % of diabetics.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: What other associations does necrobiosis lipoidica have?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: Thyroid disease and other autoimmune conditions; it can also be idiopathic.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: Does the course of necrobiosis lipoidica track glycaemic control?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: No — its presence/course doesn't reliably track glycaemic control, though you should still screen for diabetes (HbA1c/glucose).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: Where does necrobiosis lipoidica occur, and in whom?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: Bilaterally on the shins (pretibial) — the classic site — commoner in women (occasionally elsewhere).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: How does a necrobiosis lipoidica plaque evolve?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: It starts as red-brown papules → coalesces into well-demarcated plaques → becomes shiny, atrophic and yellow-brown centrally, with a raised violaceous border and visible telangiectasia.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: What is the key complication of necrobiosis lipoidica?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: Ulceration — the atrophic skin is fragile and ulcerates with minor trauma; sensation over the plaque may be reduced.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: How is necrobiosis lipoidica distinguished from diabetic dermopathy?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: Diabetic dermopathy = brown atrophic macules ('shin spots'), which are smaller and less shiny; necrobiosis lipoidica = larger shiny atrophic yellow-brown plaques with telangiectasia and a violaceous border.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: How is necrobiosis lipoidica distinguished from granuloma annulare and pretibial myxoedema?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: Granuloma annulare: annular, skin-coloured/red, no atrophy/yellow, on the dorsa of hands/feet. Pretibial myxoedema: non-pitting waxy plaques associated with Graves' disease.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: How is necrobiosis lipoidica diagnosed?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: Largely clinically (the characteristic plaque + site); screen for diabetes (HbA1c/fasting glucose); skin biopsy only if uncertain (biopsy the edge cautiously given poor healing/ulceration risk).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: What does skin biopsy show in necrobiosis lipoidica?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: Necrobiosis of collagen with palisading granulomatous inflammation.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: What is the management principle for necrobiosis lipoidica?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: It is benign but chronic and hard to treat — protect the skin + optimise diabetes/risk factors; topical/intralesional steroids first-line; escalate for refractory or ulcerated disease.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: What are the first-line/general measures in necrobiosis lipoidica?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: Optimise diabetes + cardiovascular risk factors (though this doesn't reliably improve it), stop smoking, protect the fragile skin from trauma, and use potent topical corticosteroids (to the active border) or intralesional steroids (cautiously on atrophic skin).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: What are the options for refractory or ulcerated necrobiosis lipoidica?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: Topical calcineurin inhibitors, phototherapy (PUVA), systemic agents (e.g. tetracyclines, ± TNF inhibitors); ulcerated → wound care + protection, treat secondary infection, tissue viability/dermatology input.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: What is necrolytic migratory erythema (NME)?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: A distinctive paraneoplastic dermatosis — a migratory, annular, erosive/crusted erythematous rash that is the classic cutaneous marker of a GLUCAGONOMA (a glucagon-secreting pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: What is the 'core concept' of NME?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: It is the skin's signal of an internal tumour — a paraneoplastic clue that should trigger the search for a glucagonoma; caused by hyperglucagonaemia (→ hypoaminoacidaemia ± zinc/essential fatty acid deficiency) → epidermal necrolysis.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: What is the key clinical lesson with NME?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: Recognise this specific rash → measure GLUCAGON → image the pancreas.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: What does NME point to?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: A glucagonoma (pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour) — it is the defining cutaneous component of the 'glucagonoma syndrome'.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: What are the components of the glucagonoma syndrome (the 'D's)?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: NME (the rash), Diabetes/glucose intolerance, weight loss, Anaemia (normochromic normocytic), DVT/venous thromboembolism, Depression/neuropsychiatric, Diarrhoea, and glossitis/angular stomatitis/cheilitis (± zinc/nutritional deficiency).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: Describe the rash of NME.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: Erythematous patches → annular/polycyclic plaques that MIGRATE and spread with central clearing/crusting; superficial flaccid blisters → erosion, crusting and scaling at the advancing edge; it waxes and wanes, with lesions clearing in one area and appearing in another over ~1–2 weeks.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: What is the distribution of NME?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: Intertriginous/flexural areas, the perineum and groin, the perioral region and acral sites; often painful/itchy, ± glossitis, cheilitis and angular stomatitis.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: What is the KEY diagnostic test in suspected NME?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: Serum GLUCAGON — markedly raised (diagnostic of glucagonoma) — the test the rash should trigger.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: How is the tumour localised in glucagonoma?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: CT/MRI (± endoscopic ultrasound, or a functional scan e.g. Ga-DOTATATE PET) to localise the pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour and assess for metastases (often already spread at diagnosis).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: What supporting blood tests are done in NME/glucagonoma?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: Glucose/HbA1c (diabetes), FBC (normochromic normocytic anaemia), amino acids (LOW — hypoaminoacidaemia), zinc, and chromogranin A (a neuroendocrine tumour marker).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: What does skin biopsy show in NME?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: Superficial epidermal necrolysis.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: What is the management principle for NME?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: Treat the underlying glucagonoma — the rash follows; provide supportive skin + nutritional care meanwhile.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: How is a localised glucagonoma treated, and what happens to the rash?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: Surgical resection of the glucagonoma (curative if localised) → the NME typically resolves.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: How is an unresectable/metastatic glucagonoma managed?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: Somatostatin analogues (octreotide/lanreotide) reduce glucagon and improve the rash, ± other neuroendocrine tumour therapies.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: What supportive measures accompany treatment of NME/glucagonoma?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: Correct nutritional deficiencies (amino acids, zinc, essential fatty acids — can improve the rash), manage the diabetes, give VTE prophylaxis (thromboembolism risk), and provide skin/wound care.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.front: Which nutritional deficiencies are implicated in NME?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Signs.back: Hypoaminoacidaemia (low amino acids), and zinc/essential fatty acid deficiency.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Conne.front: What is cutaneous connective tissue disease?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Conne.back: The skin manifestations of autoimmune connective tissue disease — often the presenting feature and a window onto systemic involvement.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Conne.front: What is the organising principle for cutaneous connective tissue disease?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Conne.back: The skin pattern + antibodies point to the connective tissue disease; always assess for systemic involvement (renal, lung, muscle).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Conne.front: What are the key skin signs and notes for the three main cutaneous CTDs?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Conne.back: Cutaneous lupus: malar (butterfly) rash, photosensitivity, discoid plaques → screen for SLE (ANA, dsDNA). Dermatomyositis: heliotrope rash (eyelids), Gottron's papules (knuckles), proximal myopathy, raised CK — paraneoplastic (malignancy screen). Cutaneous small-vessel vasculitis: palpable purpura (dependent areas) — look for a drug/infection trigger + systemic vasculitis.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Conne.front: Why is adult dermatomyositis important to remember?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Conne.back: It is paraneoplastic — screen for an underlying malignancy.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Conne.front: What is cutaneous lupus erythematosus (CLE)?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Conne.back: The skin manifestations of lupus — a spectrum from skin-limited disease to a cutaneous sign of systemic lupus (SLE); classic subtypes are acute CLE (malar rash), subacute CLE (SCLE) and chronic CLE (discoid lupus, DLE).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Conne.front: What is the 'core concept' of cutaneous lupus?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Conne.back: It is fundamentally a PHOTOSENSITIVE autoimmune skin disease — lesions favour sun-exposed areas and are triggered/worsened by UV.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Conne.front: What two questions dominate the assessment of cutaneous lupus?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Conne.back: (1) Which SUBTYPE? (morphology, antibodies and scarring risk differ); and (2) is there underlying SYSTEMIC lupus? — hence the workup always screens ANA + dsDNA.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Conne.front: Describe ACUTE cutaneous lupus.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Conne.back: The malar ('butterfly') rash on the cheeks/nose (sparing the nasolabial folds); non-scarring; ANA+, dsDNA+; strongly SLE-associated (part of SLE).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Conne.front: Describe SUBACUTE cutaneous lupus (SCLE).
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Conne.back: Annular/polycyclic scaly plaques, bilateral/symmetrical, on sun-exposed areas; anti-Ro/SSA positive; strongly photosensitive; NON-scarring; ~50% SLE association; can be drug-induced.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Conne.front: Describe CHRONIC (discoid) cutaneous lupus (DLE).
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Conne.back: Discoid scaly plaques on the face/scalp/ears (sun-exposed) that SCAR (scarring alopecia, atrophy, pigment change); normal serology; mostly skin-limited (low SLE association ~5–10%).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Conne.front: Which cutaneous lupus subtype scars, and why does it matter?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Conne.back: Discoid lupus (DLE) scars (scarring alopecia, atrophy, dyspigmentation) → treat early; acute and subacute CLE do not scar.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Conne.front: What is the morphology of SCLE?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Conne.back: Annular + polycyclic shapes with scale, bilateral/symmetrical, on sun-exposed areas (upper back, chest, extensor arms, neck) — photosensitive and non-scarring.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Conne.front: Which antibody is associated with SCLE?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Conne.back: Anti-Ro/SSA (ENA-Ro) positive.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Conne.front: Which drugs can induce SCLE?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Conne.back: Hydrochlorothiazide, terbinafine, PPIs and some antihypertensives — always ask about drugs.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Conne.front: Why must you screen for SLE in any cutaneous lupus?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Conne.back: Because CLE may signal systemic lupus — assess for systemic features (arthralgia, fatigue, oral ulcers, serositis, renal/haematological involvement) and screen ANA + dsDNA.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Conne.front: What are the serology findings in SCLE vs DLE?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Conne.back: SCLE: anti-Ro/SSA positive; DLE: normal serology; always also screen ANA + dsDNA for underlying SLE.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Conne.front: What does skin biopsy show in cutaneous lupus?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Conne.back: Interface dermatitis, ± a lupus band on immunofluorescence (confirming the diagnosis).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Conne.front: Which investigations are done if SLE is suspected in cutaneous lupus?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Conne.back: FBC, U&Es, urinalysis, complement (C3/C4), and anti-Ro/La (relevant in pregnancy — neonatal lupus/congenital heart block risk).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Conne.front: What is the cornerstone of management for cutaneous lupus?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Cutaneous Conne.back: Sun protection (high-factor sunscreen, sun avoidance, protective clothing) + vitamin D supplementation.
