options: Urgent referral and investigation for an underlying malignancy
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Seborrhoeic Ker.answer: Urgent referral and investigation for an underlying malignancy
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Seborrhoeic Ker.explanation: A sudden eruption of seborrhoeic keratoses (Leser-Trélat) with weight loss/GI symptoms warrants urgent referral and investigation for internal malignancy.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Seborrhoeic Ker.question: Which removal method is commonly used for a symptomatic seborrhoeic keratosis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Seborrhoeic Ker.explanation: Symptomatic seborrhoeic keratoses can be removed by cryotherapy, curettage + cautery or shave excision.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Seborrhoeic Ker.question: Which feature is present in a seborrhoeic keratosis but NOT typically in melanoma?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Seborrhoeic Ker.explanation: Keratin (horn) cysts are a benign feature of seborrhoeic keratoses, not typical of melanoma, which shows irregular/changing features.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.question: A 45-year-old fair-skinned woman has central facial redness with flushing, visible small blood vessels and some papules and pustules on the cheeks and nose, but NO blackheads or whiteheads. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.explanation: Central facial flushing, persistent erythema, telangiectasia and papules/pustules WITHOUT comedones in a fair-skinned 30–50-year-old is rosacea.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.question: What is the KEY feature that distinguishes rosacea from acne?
options: The absence of comedones (and the presence of flushing/telangiectasia)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.answer: The absence of comedones (and the presence of flushing/telangiectasia)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.explanation: Rosacea has no comedones (and has flushing/telangiectasia), whereas acne has comedones ± cysts.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.question: Which change, a late phymatous feature of rosacea, mainly affects men?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.explanation: Rhinophyma — a thickened, bulbous nose from sebaceous/connective tissue overgrowth — is a late feature of rosacea, mainly in men.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.question: A patient with rosacea reports eye pain, photophobia and blurred vision. What is the appropriate action?
options: Urgent ophthalmology referral (risk of sight-threatening keratitis)
Prescribe a topical steroid to the eye
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.answer: Urgent ophthalmology referral (risk of sight-threatening keratitis)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.explanation: Eye pain, photophobia or visual change in rosacea signals keratitis (sight-threatening), warranting urgent ophthalmology referral.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.question: Which treatment should be AVOIDED in rosacea because it worsens it?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.explanation: Topical corticosteroids worsen rosacea (steroid-induced rosacea/rebound) and should be avoided.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.question: What is the first-line topical treatment for the papules/pustules of rosacea?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.explanation: Topical ivermectin is first-line for the papules/pustules of rosacea (with metronidazole or azelaic acid as alternatives).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.question: How is moderate-severe papulopustular rosacea treated systemically?
options: An oral tetracycline (doxycycline/lymecycline) at an anti-inflammatory dose
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.answer: An oral tetracycline (doxycycline/lymecycline) at an anti-inflammatory dose
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.explanation: Moderate-severe papulopustular rosacea is treated with an oral tetracycline at an anti-inflammatory (not antibacterial) dose.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.question: Which topical agent is used for the persistent erythema of rosacea?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.explanation: Topical brimonidine (or oxymetazoline), an α-agonist vasoconstrictor, reduces the persistent erythema of rosacea.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.question: Which is a recognised trigger of rosacea flushing?
options: Heat, sun, alcohol, spicy food and stress
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.answer: Heat, sun, alcohol, spicy food and stress
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.explanation: Heat, sun/UV, hot drinks, alcohol, spicy food, stress and exercise are recognised triggers of rosacea.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.question: How do oral tetracyclines act in rosacea?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.explanation: In rosacea, oral tetracyclines work as anti-inflammatory agents rather than as antibacterials.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.question: How are telangiectasia and rhinophyma treated in rosacea?
options: Vascular laser/IPL (telangiectasia) and surgery/laser (rhinophyma), via specialist referral
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.answer: Vascular laser/IPL (telangiectasia) and surgery/laser (rhinophyma), via specialist referral
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.explanation: Telangiectasia is treated with vascular laser/IPL and rhinophyma with surgery/laser, both via specialist referral.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.question: What general measure applies to ALL patients with rosacea?
options: Trigger avoidance, daily sunscreen (SPF ≥30) and gentle skincare (avoid topical steroids)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.answer: Trigger avoidance, daily sunscreen (SPF ≥30) and gentle skincare (avoid topical steroids)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.explanation: All rosacea patients should avoid triggers, use daily sunscreen (SPF ≥30) and gentle skincare, and avoid topical steroids.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.question: What is the expected treatment timescale for rosacea?
options: Review at ~6 weeks but expect to need at least 3 months (it responds slowly)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.answer: Review at ~6 weeks but expect to need at least 3 months (it responds slowly)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.explanation: Rosacea responds slowly — review at ~6 weeks, but at least 3 months of treatment is usually needed.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.question: A patient develops a rash of papules and pustules around the mouth after using a potent topical steroid on the face. Which diagnosis is this, rather than rosacea?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.explanation: Papules/pustules around the mouth, often topical-steroid-induced, suggest perioral dermatitis (a differential of rosacea).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.question: Which treatment is reserved for refractory papulopustular rosacea?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.explanation: Low-dose oral isotretinoin (specialist-initiated) is used for refractory papulopustular rosacea.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.question: Which patient group is most predisposed to rosacea?
options: Fair/Celtic-skinned adults aged 30–50 with blue eyes
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.answer: Fair/Celtic-skinned adults aged 30–50 with blue eyes
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.explanation: Rosacea most affects fair/Celtic-skinned adults aged 30–50 (women more, but men get rhinophyma).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.question: Which ocular features are seen in ocular rosacea?
options: Dry, gritty, red eyes with blepharitis, styes/chalazia and lid-margin telangiectasia
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.answer: Dry, gritty, red eyes with blepharitis, styes/chalazia and lid-margin telangiectasia
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea.explanation: Ocular rosacea causes dry, gritty, red eyes, blepharitis, conjunctivitis, styes/chalazia and lid-margin telangiectasia (red flags: pain/photophobia/visual change).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.question: A young adult has well-demarcated, salmon-pink plaques with overlying silvery scale symmetrically on the elbows, knees and scalp. Scraping the scale produces pinpoint bleeding. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.explanation: Well-demarcated salmon-pink plaques with silvery scale on extensor surfaces/scalp and a positive Auspitz sign are chronic plaque psoriasis.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.question: What is the underlying mechanism of psoriasis?
options: T-cell inflammation driving keratinocyte hyperproliferation (rapid epidermal turnover)
IgA deposition at the dermal papillae
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.answer: T-cell inflammation driving keratinocyte hyperproliferation (rapid epidermal turnover)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.explanation: Psoriasis is T-cell-mediated inflammation causing accelerated keratinocyte turnover, producing thick scaly plaques.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.question: A child develops crops of small 'raindrop' scaly papules two weeks after a sore throat. Which type of psoriasis is this?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.explanation: Guttate psoriasis presents with small raindrop papules in young patients following a streptococcal throat infection.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.question: Which sign describes pinpoint bleeding when psoriatic scale is scraped away?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.explanation: The Auspitz sign is pinpoint bleeding on scraping the scale, from the thin epidermis over dilated dermal capillaries.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.question: Which nail changes are characteristic of psoriasis and predict psoriatic arthritis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.explanation: Nail pitting, onycholysis and subungual hyperkeratosis are characteristic of psoriasis and predict psoriatic arthritis.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.question: Which drug is a recognised trigger of psoriasis?
options: Lithium (also beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors, antimalarials, NSAIDs)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.answer: Lithium (also beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors, antimalarials, NSAIDs)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.explanation: Lithium, beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors, antimalarials and NSAIDs are recognised drug triggers of psoriasis.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.question: Why should systemic corticosteroids be avoided in chronic plaque psoriasis?
options: Their withdrawal can precipitate a pustular or erythrodermic flare
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.answer: Their withdrawal can precipitate a pustular or erythrodermic flare
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.explanation: Systemic steroid withdrawal can precipitate pustular/erythrodermic psoriasis, so systemic steroids are avoided.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.question: What is the NICE first-line topical regimen for trunk/limb plaque psoriasis?
options: A potent topical steroid once daily plus a vitamin D analogue once daily, applied separately, for up to 4 weeks
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.answer: A potent topical steroid once daily plus a vitamin D analogue once daily, applied separately, for up to 4 weeks
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.explanation: NICE first-line for trunk/limb plaque psoriasis is a potent topical steroid once daily plus a vitamin D analogue (calcipotriol) once daily, applied separately, for up to 4 weeks.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.question: Which types of psoriasis are dermatological EMERGENCIES?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.explanation: Generalised pustular psoriasis and erythrodermic psoriasis are dermatological emergencies (skin failure).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.question: Which systemic disease association should always be asked about in psoriasis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.explanation: Psoriatic arthritis occurs in a significant minority, so joints should always be asked about (e.g. PEST screening).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.question: A patient has smooth, shiny, non-scaly red plaques in the axillae and groin. Which type of psoriasis is this?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.explanation: Flexural (inverse) psoriasis gives smooth, shiny, non-scaly red plaques in skin folds where the scale is rubbed off.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.question: How does sunlight generally affect psoriasis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.explanation: Sunlight usually relieves psoriasis (rarely exacerbating it), and phototherapy is a treatment.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.question: Which phenomenon (lesions at sites of trauma) is seen in psoriasis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.explanation: Psoriasis shows the Koebner phenomenon — new lesions at sites of skin injury/trauma (shared with lichen planus and vitiligo).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.question: Which is an appropriate escalation for severe/refractory psoriasis after topicals and phototherapy?
options: Systemic agents (methotrexate, ciclosporin, acitretin) or biologics
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.answer: Systemic agents (methotrexate, ciclosporin, acitretin) or biologics
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.explanation: Severe/refractory psoriasis is escalated to systemic agents (methotrexate/ciclosporin/acitretin) and then biologics (anti-TNF/IL-17/IL-23).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.question: How is scalp psoriasis treated first-line?
options: A potent topical steroid once daily (up to 4 weeks), then a combined calcipotriol/betamethasone gel
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.answer: A potent topical steroid once daily (up to 4 weeks), then a combined calcipotriol/betamethasone gel
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.explanation: Scalp psoriasis is treated with a potent topical steroid once daily (up to 4 weeks), then a combined calcipotriol/betamethasone gel.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.question: What lifestyle advice applies to ALL patients with psoriasis (alongside emollients)?
options: Stop smoking and reduce alcohol, with cardiovascular risk assessment
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.answer: Stop smoking and reduce alcohol, with cardiovascular risk assessment
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.explanation: All psoriasis patients should have emollients plus lifestyle advice (stop smoking, reduce alcohol) and cardiovascular risk assessment.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.question: Which biologic class targets IL-17 in psoriasis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.explanation: Secukinumab is an anti-IL-17 biologic used in severe psoriasis (anti-TNF, anti-IL-23 and anti-IL-12/23 are other classes).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.question: Which topical add-on helps descale thick psoriatic plaques?
options: Salicylic acid or urea (± coal tar, dithranol short-contact)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.answer: Salicylic acid or urea (± coal tar, dithranol short-contact)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.explanation: Salicylic acid/urea (descaling), coal tar and short-contact dithranol are add-ons for thick psoriatic plaques.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.question: How is guttate psoriasis managed when a streptococcal infection is proven?
options: Narrowband UVB plus antibiotics for the streptococcal infection
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.answer: Narrowband UVB plus antibiotics for the streptococcal infection
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis.explanation: Guttate psoriasis is managed with narrowband UVB and antibiotics if a streptococcal infection is proven (it may also self-resolve).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.question: A 40-year-old has intensely itchy, violaceous, flat-topped polygonal papules on the flexor wrists and ankles, with fine white lace-like lines on their surface. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.explanation: Purple, pruritic, polygonal, planar papules with Wickham's striae on the flexor wrists/ankles are lichen planus.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.question: What are 'Wickham's striae'?
options: Fine white lace-like lines on the surface of the papules (and oral lesions)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.answer: Fine white lace-like lines on the surface of the papules (and oral lesions)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.explanation: Wickham's striae are fine white lace-like surface lines, a near-pathognomonic sign of lichen planus.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.question: What is the underlying mechanism of lichen planus?
options: A T-cell attack on basal keratinocytes (a lichenoid interface reaction)
IgA deposition at the dermal papillae
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.answer: A T-cell attack on basal keratinocytes (a lichenoid interface reaction)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.explanation: Lichen planus is a T-cell-mediated attack on the basal keratinocytes — a lichenoid interface reaction.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.question: Which oral finding is characteristic of lichen planus?
options: Lacy white reticular (Wickham's) striae on the buccal mucosa
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.answer: Lacy white reticular (Wickham's) striae on the buccal mucosa
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.explanation: Lacy white reticular Wickham's striae on the buccal mucosa are characteristic of oral lichen planus.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.question: Which nail change is seen in lichen planus?
options: Pterygium (dorsal scarring), with longitudinal ridging and thinning
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.answer: Pterygium (dorsal scarring), with longitudinal ridging and thinning
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.explanation: Lichen planus can cause nail pterygium (dorsal scarring), longitudinal ridging and thinning.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.question: Which infection is lichen planus associated with (warranting screening in oral/atypical disease)?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.explanation: Lichen planus (especially oral/erosive) is associated with hepatitis C (± B), so screening should be considered.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.question: Which drug is a recognised cause of a lichenoid (drug-induced) eruption?
options: A thiazide diuretic (also antimalarials, anticonvulsants, NSAIDs, penicillamine)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.answer: A thiazide diuretic (also antimalarials, anticonvulsants, NSAIDs, penicillamine)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.explanation: Thiazides (and antimalarials, anticonvulsants, NSAIDs, penicillamine) can cause a lichenoid drug eruption, which resolves on stopping the drug.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.question: What is the malignant potential of lichen planus?
options: Erosive oral/genital disease is a potentially malignant disorder (~1% SCC transformation)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.answer: Erosive oral/genital disease is a potentially malignant disorder (~1% SCC transformation)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.explanation: Erosive oral and genital lichen planus is a potentially malignant disorder, with ~1% SCC transformation (oral) — monitor and biopsy non-healing areas.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.question: Which histological features are seen in lichen planus?
options: 'Saw-tooth' rete ridges with a band-like lymphocytic infiltrate and basal degeneration
Acantholysis with a tombstone basal layer
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.answer: 'Saw-tooth' rete ridges with a band-like lymphocytic infiltrate and basal degeneration
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.explanation: Lichen planus shows saw-tooth rete ridges, a band-like (lichenoid) lymphocytic infiltrate and basal degeneration.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.question: What is the FIRST-line treatment for cutaneous lichen planus?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.explanation: Potent topical corticosteroids are first-line for lichen planus (± topical calcineurin inhibitors for oral/genital disease).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.question: Lichen planus of the scalp causing scarring alopecia is called:
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.explanation: Lichen planopilaris is lichen planus of the scalp, causing a scarring (permanent) alopecia.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.question: Which phenomenon (lesions appearing at sites of trauma) is shared by lichen planus, psoriasis and vitiligo?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.explanation: The Koebner phenomenon (lesions at trauma sites) is shared by lichen planus, psoriasis and vitiligo.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.question: What is the typical natural history of cutaneous lichen planus?
options: Often self-limiting, resolving over ~1–2 years (may leave post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.answer: Often self-limiting, resolving over ~1–2 years (may leave post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.explanation: Cutaneous lichen planus is often self-limiting over ~1–2 years, sometimes leaving post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation; mucosal/scalp disease tends to be chronic.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.question: A patient develops a widespread, atypical lichenoid eruption after starting a new antihypertensive. What should be considered?
options: A drug-induced (lichenoid) eruption — resolves on stopping the drug
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.answer: A drug-induced (lichenoid) eruption — resolves on stopping the drug
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.explanation: A widespread/atypical lichenoid eruption temporally related to a drug suggests a drug-induced lichenoid eruption, which resolves on stopping the culprit.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.question: Which body sites should always be examined in a patient with lichen planus?
options: The mouth, genitals, nails and scalp
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.answer: The mouth, genitals, nails and scalp
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.explanation: Lichen planus is multi-site, so the mouth (striae/erosive), genitals, nails (pterygium) and scalp (scarring alopecia) should be checked.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.question: Which is an appropriate escalation for severe/refractory lichen planus?
options: Immunosuppressants (azathioprine, methotrexate or mycophenolate), or oral retinoids/phototherapy
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.answer: Immunosuppressants (azathioprine, methotrexate or mycophenolate), or oral retinoids/phototherapy
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.explanation: Severe/refractory lichen planus is escalated to phototherapy, short oral steroids, oral retinoids (acitretin) or immunosuppressants (azathioprine/methotrexate/mycophenolate).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.question: At what age does lichen planus typically present?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.explanation: Lichen planus typically presents between the ages of 20 and 50.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.question: Which variant of lichen planus is thick, very itchy, and typically on the shins?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus.explanation: Hypertrophic lichen planus presents as thick, very itchy plaques, typically on the shins.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.question: An elderly obese woman with varicose veins has a shallow, exudative ulcer around the medial malleolus, with brown pigmentation and hardened 'inverted champagne bottle' lower legs. It is less painful and improves on elevation. ABPI is 0.9. What is the diagnosis and management?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.answer: Venous ulcer — compression
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.explanation: A gaiter-region shallow exudative ulcer with haemosiderin/lipodermatosclerosis, less painful, ABPI >0.8, is a venous ulcer — managed with compression.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.question: What is the MASTER decision when assessing a leg ulcer?
options: Venous vs arterial (because compression heals venous but is dangerous in arterial)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.answer: Venous vs arterial (because compression heals venous but is dangerous in arterial)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.explanation: Venous vs arterial is the master decision — compression is the cornerstone of venous healing but is limb-threatening in arterial disease.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.question: Why must an ABPI be checked before applying compression to a leg ulcer?
options: To exclude significant arterial disease (compression on an arterial ulcer causes ischaemia)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.answer: To exclude significant arterial disease (compression on an arterial ulcer causes ischaemia)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.explanation: ABPI is mandatory before compression to exclude arterial disease, as compressing an arterial ulcer worsens ischaemia and risks limb loss.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.question: Which ABPI range allows safe full (multi-component) compression for a venous ulcer?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.explanation: An ABPI of 0.8–1.3 allows safe full compression, the cornerstone of venous ulcer healing.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.question: A painful, deep, 'punched-out' ulcer on the dorsum of the foot, with cold, pale, hairless skin and absent pulses (worse on elevation), has an ABPI of 0.6. What is the management?
options: Do NOT compress; urgent vascular referral for revascularisation + cardiovascular risk management
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.answer: Do NOT compress; urgent vascular referral for revascularisation + cardiovascular risk management
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.explanation: A painful distal punched-out ulcer with absent pulses and ABPI <0.8 is arterial — never compress; refer urgently for revascularisation and manage cardiovascular risk.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.question: Which skin changes are characteristic of chronic venous hypertension?
options: Haemosiderin deposition, lipodermatosclerosis and varicose eczema
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.answer: Haemosiderin deposition, lipodermatosclerosis and varicose eczema
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.explanation: Venous hypertension causes haemosiderin deposition, lipodermatosclerosis ('inverted champagne bottle') and varicose eczema.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.question: A diabetic patient has a painless, punched-out ulcer under the metatarsal head, surrounded by callus, with a warm well-perfused foot. What type of ulcer is this?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.answer: Neuropathic (diabetic)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.explanation: A painless ulcer at a pressure point with surrounding callus and a warm perfused foot in a diabetic is a neuropathic ulcer.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.question: How should a neuropathic (diabetic) foot ulcer be managed?
options: Diabetic foot MDT, pressure offloading, glycaemic control, debridement and treat infection
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.answer: Diabetic foot MDT, pressure offloading, glycaemic control, debridement and treat infection
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.explanation: Neuropathic ulcers are managed with a diabetic foot MDT, offloading, glycaemic control, debridement and infection treatment.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.question: What is the safest statement about compression and arterial ulcers?
options: Never apply compression to an arterial (or significantly mixed) ulcer — it worsens ischaemia
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.answer: Never apply compression to an arterial (or significantly mixed) ulcer — it worsens ischaemia
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.explanation: Compression must never be applied to an arterial (or significantly mixed) ulcer, as it worsens ischaemia and risks tissue necrosis/limb loss.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.question: Which trial supports early endovenous ablation to improve venous ulcer healing and reduce recurrence?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.answer: EVRA trial
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.explanation: The EVRA trial supports early endovenous ablation to improve venous ulcer healing and reduce recurrence.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.question: According to NICE NG152, when should topical antibiotics/antiseptics be used on a venous ulcer?
options: Only if the ulcer is clinically infected
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.answer: Only if the ulcer is clinically infected
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.explanation: NICE NG152 advises avoiding routine topical antibiotics/antiseptics — use them only if the ulcer is clinically infected.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.question: A chronic non-healing leg ulcer develops a rolled/everted edge with abnormal granulation. What should be done?
options: Biopsy to exclude a Marjolin's ulcer (SCC in a chronic wound)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.answer: Biopsy to exclude a Marjolin's ulcer (SCC in a chronic wound)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.explanation: Chronic/atypical non-healing ulcers with rolled/everted edges should be biopsied to exclude a Marjolin's ulcer (SCC).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.question: An ABPI of >1.3–1.4 in a diabetic patient with a leg ulcer indicates what?
options: Calcified/incompressible vessels — the ABPI is unreliable; refer (use toe pressures)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.answer: Calcified/incompressible vessels — the ABPI is unreliable; refer (use toe pressures)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.explanation: An ABPI >1.3–1.4 suggests calcified/incompressible vessels (diabetes/CKD), making it unreliable — refer and use toe pressures/vascular review.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.question: How is a mixed arterial-venous ulcer (ABPI 0.5–0.8) managed?
options: Reduced compression only under specialist supervision, treating both components
No compression ever, and no venous treatment
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.answer: Reduced compression only under specialist supervision, treating both components
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.explanation: Mixed ulcers (ABPI 0.5–0.8) may have reduced compression only under specialist supervision, treating both the arterial and venous components.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.question: Which is the commonest type of leg ulcer?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.answer: Venous (~70%)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.explanation: Venous ulcers are the commonest type of leg ulcer (~70%).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.question: Besides revascularisation, what is essential in managing an arterial ulcer?
options: Cardiovascular risk management (smoking cessation, statin, antiplatelet, BP/diabetes control)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.answer: Cardiovascular risk management (smoking cessation, statin, antiplatelet, BP/diabetes control)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.explanation: Arterial ulcers require cardiovascular risk management — smoking cessation, statin, antiplatelet and BP/diabetes control — alongside revascularisation.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.question: When should a venous ulcer be referred for specialist assessment?
options: If persisting >2 weeks / non-healing at 12 weeks / atypical / suspected arterial or mixed / recurrent
Only if the patient requests it
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.answer: If persisting >2 weeks / non-healing at 12 weeks / atypical / suspected arterial or mixed / recurrent
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.explanation: Referral is indicated for a venous ulcer persisting >2 weeks, non-healing at 12 weeks, atypical, suspected arterial/mixed, or recurrent.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.question: Which pain pattern distinguishes an arterial ulcer?
options: Painful, worse on elevation and at night, relieved by hanging the leg down
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.answer: Painful, worse on elevation and at night, relieved by hanging the leg down
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.explanation: Arterial ulcers are painful, worse on elevation and at night, and relieved by hanging the leg down (dependency), reflecting ischaemia.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.question: An immobile elderly patient develops a full-thickness sacral ulcer with visible subcutaneous fat but no exposed bone, tendon or muscle. What category is this?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.answer: Category 3
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.explanation: Full-thickness skin loss with visible subcutaneous fat, but no exposed bone/tendon/muscle, is a Category 3 pressure ulcer.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.question: A pressure ulcer with non-blanchable erythema of intact skin is which category?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.answer: Category 1
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.explanation: Non-blanchable erythema of intact skin is a Category 1 pressure ulcer.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.question: A pressure ulcer with exposed, palpable bone is which category?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.answer: Category 4
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.explanation: Exposed/palpable bone, tendon or muscle indicates a Category 4 pressure ulcer.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.question: What is the biggest risk factor for pressure ulcers?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.answer: Immobility
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.explanation: Immobility is the biggest risk factor for pressure ulcers (bed/chair-bound, paralysis, sedation, surgery).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.question: Which are the classic sites of pressure ulcers?
options: The sacrum, heels, ischial tuberosities and greater trochanters
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.answer: The sacrum, heels, ischial tuberosities and greater trochanters
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.explanation: Pressure ulcers classically occur over bony prominences — sacrum, heels, ischial tuberosities and greater trochanters (also occiput, elbows, malleoli).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.question: Which validated tool is used (with clinical judgement) to assess pressure ulcer risk?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.answer: The Waterlow score (or Braden/Norton)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.explanation: Pressure ulcer risk is assessed with a validated tool such as Waterlow (or Braden/Norton) alongside clinical judgement.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.question: Which action is NOT recommended to prevent pressure ulcers (NICE CG179)?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.answer: Skin massage/rubbing over bony prominences
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.explanation: NICE CG179 advises against using skin massage/rubbing to prevent pressure ulcers.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.question: A stable, dry, intact eschar is present on a patient's heel. What is the correct management?
options: Do NOT remove it — it acts as a natural biological cover
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.answer: Do NOT remove it — it acts as a natural biological cover
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.explanation: Stable, dry, intact heel eschar should not be removed, as it acts as a natural biological cover.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.question: What does the SSKIN bundle stand for?
options: Surface, Skin inspection, Keep moving, Incontinence/moisture, Nutrition
Surface, Steroids, Keep dry, Infection, NSAIDs
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.answer: Skin, Steroids, Kidney, Infection, Nutrition
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.explanation: SSKIN = Surface, Skin inspection, Keep moving, Incontinence/moisture and Nutrition — the pressure ulcer prevention bundle.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.question: When should systemic antibiotics be used for a pressure ulcer?
options: Only for clinical infection (spreading erythema, cellulitis, systemic upset, suspected osteomyelitis)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.answer: Only for clinical infection (spreading erythema, cellulitis, systemic upset, suspected osteomyelitis)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.explanation: Systemic antibiotics are reserved for clinical infection (not routine or for colonisation) — treat infection, not colonisation.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.question: A deep sacral pressure ulcer over bone is not healing and the patient is systemically unwell. Which complication should be suspected?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.answer: Osteomyelitis
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.explanation: A deep, non-healing pressure ulcer over bone with systemic upset should raise suspicion of osteomyelitis (also cellulitis/sepsis).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.question: Why must prevention be continued even after a pressure ulcer develops?
options: The ulcer won't heal under continued pressure
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.answer: The ulcer won't heal under continued pressure
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.explanation: All prevention (offloading/repositioning) must continue, because the ulcer cannot heal if pressure is sustained.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.question: A pressure ulcer's depth is obscured by slough and eschar so it cannot be categorised. How is it classified?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.answer: Unstageable
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.explanation: A full-thickness ulcer whose depth is obscured by slough or eschar is classified as 'unstageable'.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.question: In a patient with darker skin, how should Category 1 pressure damage be assessed beyond colour?
options: Also assess skin temperature, firmness/oedema and pain
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.answer: Also assess skin temperature, firmness/oedema and pain
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.explanation: Non-blanchable erythema is harder to see in darker skin, so also assess skin temperature, firmness/oedema and pain.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.question: What is the appropriate surgical management for a large or deep (Category 3–4) non-healing pressure ulcer?
options: Surgical review for debridement or flap reconstruction
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.answer: Surgical review for debridement or flap reconstruction
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.explanation: Large/deep (Category 3–4) or non-healing pressure ulcers warrant surgical review for debridement or flap reconstruction, alongside tissue viability input.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.question: Which purple/maroon localised area of intact or non-intact skin (or a blood blister) describes:
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.answer: A deep tissue injury
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.explanation: A localised purple/maroon area or blood blister of intact/non-intact skin is a deep tissue injury (pressure).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.question: When should skin integrity first be assessed for pressure ulcer risk after admission (NICE CG179)?
options: Within 6 hours of admission (and on any change)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.answer: Within 6 hours of admission (and on any change)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.explanation: NICE CG179 advises assessing skin integrity within 6 hours of admission and on any change in condition.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.question: A pressure ulcer develops that appears avoidable. What administrative step is required?
options: Document and report it as a patient-safety incident (± safeguarding review)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.answer: Document and report it as a patient-safety incident (± safeguarding review)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pr.explanation: Pressure ulcers are a patient-safety marker; they should be documented and reported as incidents, with a safeguarding review if avoidable.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: An 80-year-old presents with very itchy, tense, robust blisters on the arms and legs, some preceded by urticated plaques. The mouth is not involved and Nikolsky's sign is negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: Tense, itchy blisters with a negative Nikolsky and spared mucosa in an elderly patient are bullous pemphigoid (a deep sub-epidermal split).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: Which proteins are targeted in bullous pemphigoid?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: Bullous pemphigoid antibodies target the hemidesmosome proteins BP180 and BP230 at the basement membrane.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: Why are the blisters of bullous pemphigoid TENSE (unlike pemphigus)?
options: The split is deep (sub-epidermal), so the full-thickness epidermis forms an intact roof
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.answer: The split is deep (sub-epidermal), so the full-thickness epidermis forms an intact roof
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: The deep sub-epidermal split leaves an intact epidermal roof, producing tense, robust blisters (vs flaccid in the superficial pemphigus split).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: Is Nikolsky's sign positive or negative in bullous pemphigoid?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: Nikolsky's sign is negative in bullous pemphigoid because the split is deep with an intact roof (it is positive in pemphigus).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: How does bullous pemphigoid differ from pemphigus vulgaris regarding mucosa and age?
options: Pemphigoid involves mucosa in the young
Pemphigoid usually spares mucosa and affects the elderly; pemphigus involves mucosa and affects middle-aged patients
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.answer: Pemphigoid usually spares mucosa and affects the elderly; pemphigus involves mucosa and affects middle-aged patients
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: Bullous pemphigoid usually spares mucosa and affects the elderly, whereas pemphigus vulgaris involves the mucosa and affects middle-aged patients.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: Which memory hook helps distinguish pemphigoid from pemphigus?
options: 'The deeper the antibody, the tenser the blister' (pemphigoid = deep/tense; pemphigus = superficial/flaccid)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.answer: 'The deeper the antibody, the tenser the blister' (pemphigoid = deep/tense; pemphigus = superficial/flaccid)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: The hook 'the deeper the antibody, the tenser the blister' captures pemphigoid (deep/tense) vs pemphigus (superficial/flaccid).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: Which class of diabetes drug is a recognised trigger of bullous pemphigoid?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: Gliptins (DPP-4 inhibitors) are a recognised drug trigger of bullous pemphigoid (as are PD-1 inhibitors).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: Which condition is bullous pemphigoid associated with?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: Bullous pemphigoid is associated with neurological disease (stroke, dementia, Parkinson's) in the elderly, and uncommonly malignancy.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: What does direct immunofluorescence show in bullous pemphigoid?
options: Linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane
Granular IgA at the dermal papillae
Linear IgA at the basement membrane only
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.answer: Linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: Bullous pemphigoid shows linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane on direct immunofluorescence.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: Which pattern of immunofluorescence corresponds to pemphigus?
options: Linear IgG/C3 at the basement membrane
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: Pemphigus shows intercellular IgG ('chicken-wire') deposition, unlike the linear basement-membrane pattern of pemphigoid.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: What is the first-line treatment for localised bullous pemphigoid?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: A super-potent topical steroid (e.g. clobetasol) is first-line, especially for localised bullous pemphigoid — as effective and safer than oral steroids.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: The BLISTER trial supported which systemic option as a safer first-line for many patients with bullous pemphigoid?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: The BLISTER trial supported doxycycline as a safer first-line systemic option (vs oral steroid) for many patients with bullous pemphigoid.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: Which histological finding is seen on lesional biopsy in bullous pemphigoid?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: Bullous pemphigoid shows a sub-epidermal blister with eosinophils on lesional histology.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: A tense blister in bullous pemphigoid becomes large. What is the appropriate skin-care step?
options: Leave it and apply an adhesive dressing
Deroof/aspirate it and leave the roof as a dressing (with non-adhesive dressings ± potassium permanganate soaks)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.answer: Deroof/aspirate it and leave the roof as a dressing (with non-adhesive dressings ± potassium permanganate soaks)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: Large tense blisters can be deroofed/aspirated with the roof left as a dressing, alongside non-adhesive dressings and potassium permanganate soaks for weeping skin.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: Which is the commonest autoimmune blistering disease?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: Bullous pemphigoid is the commonest autoimmune blistering disease, typically in the elderly.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: A middle-aged patient has flaccid, easily-ruptured blisters with painful oral erosions and a positive Nikolsky sign. Which diagnosis is this, rather than bullous pemphigoid?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: Flaccid blisters with mucosal erosions and a positive Nikolsky in a middle-aged patient are pemphigus vulgaris (a superficial intra-epidermal split), not bullous pemphigoid.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: Which treatment is reserved for refractory bullous pemphigoid?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: Rituximab is used for refractory bullous pemphigoid, after topical/systemic steroids, doxycycline and steroid-sparing agents (methotrexate/mycophenolate).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: A 50-year-old presents with painful, non-healing mouth erosions for two months, and now has flaccid skin blisters that rupture easily to leave raw erosions. Nikolsky's sign is positive. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: Painful oral erosions first, flaccid rupturing blisters and a positive Nikolsky in a middle-aged patient are pemphigus vulgaris.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: Which proteins are targeted in pemphigus vulgaris?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: Pemphigus vulgaris antibodies target desmoglein 1 and 3 (desmosomal cadherins), causing acantholysis.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: Why are the blisters in pemphigus vulgaris FLACCID and rupture easily?
options: The intra-epidermal (superficial) split leaves only a thin, fragile roof
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.answer: The intra-epidermal (superficial) split leaves only a thin, fragile roof
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: The superficial intra-epidermal split (acantholysis) leaves a thin fragile roof, so blisters are flaccid and rupture almost immediately.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: Is Nikolsky's sign positive or negative in pemphigus vulgaris?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: Nikolsky's sign is positive in pemphigus vulgaris because of the superficial intra-epidermal split.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: Which feature is often the FIRST manifestation of pemphigus vulgaris?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: Painful, non-healing oral erosions are often the first (and sometimes only) feature of pemphigus vulgaris, preceding skin disease by months.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: What does direct immunofluorescence show in pemphigus vulgaris?
options: Linear IgG/C3 at the basement membrane
Granular IgA at the dermal papillae
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: Pemphigus vulgaris shows intercellular IgG ('chicken-wire') deposition throughout the epidermis.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: What histological finding characterises pemphigus vulgaris?
options: Intra-epidermal split with acantholysis ('tombstone' basal layer)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.answer: Intra-epidermal split with acantholysis ('tombstone' basal layer)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: Pemphigus vulgaris shows an intra-epidermal split with acantholysis (separated keratinocytes; a 'tombstone' basal layer).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: Which serum antibody tracks disease activity in pemphigus vulgaris?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: Serum anti-desmoglein 1 and 3 (ELISA) tracks disease activity in pemphigus vulgaris.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: What is the mainstay of treatment for pemphigus vulgaris?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: Pemphigus vulgaris needs systemic immunosuppression — corticosteroids (the mainstay) with rituximab/azathioprine/mycophenolate; topical treatment alone is insufficient.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: Which biologic is increasingly used first-line (with steroids) for moderate-severe pemphigus vulgaris?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: Rituximab (anti-CD20 B-cell depletion) is increasingly first-line with steroids for moderate-severe pemphigus vulgaris.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: Why does pemphigus vulgaris cause prominent MUCOSAL disease?
options: Desmoglein-3 is expressed in the mucosa and deep epidermis, so anti-Dsg3 causes mucosal erosions
It is caused by a virus
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.answer: Desmoglein-3 is expressed in the mucosa and deep epidermis, so anti-Dsg3 causes mucosal erosions
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: Desmoglein-3 is expressed in the mucosa (and deep epidermis), so anti-Dsg3 antibodies cause prominent mucosal (mouth) erosions.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: Which drug is a recognised cause of drug-induced pemphigus?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: Penicillamine and ACE inhibitors are recognised causes of drug-induced pemphigus.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: Which symptom predominates in pemphigus vulgaris, distinguishing it from bullous pemphigoid?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: Pemphigus vulgaris erosions are painful, whereas bullous pemphigoid is characteristically itchy.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: A patient has chronic, painful, non-healing mouth ulceration for months with no clear cause. Which serious diagnosis should be considered?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: Chronic painful non-healing mouth erosions can be the first feature of pemphigus vulgaris and should prompt consideration and biopsy.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: At what age does pemphigus vulgaris typically present, compared with bullous pemphigoid?
options: Middle age (40–60), whereas pemphigoid is in the elderly (>60)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.answer: Middle age (40–60), whereas pemphigoid is in the elderly (>60)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: Pemphigus vulgaris typically presents in middle age (40–60), whereas bullous pemphigoid affects the elderly (>60).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: Which supportive issue must be actively managed in pemphigus vulgaris due to painful mouth erosions?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: Painful mouth erosions impair intake, so fluid and nutrition must be managed, alongside treating secondary infection and monitoring immunosuppression.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: A young adult has intensely itchy, grouped small vesicles and excoriations symmetrically on the elbows, knees and buttocks. Direct immunofluorescence shows granular IgA in the dermal papillae. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: Intensely itchy grouped vesicles on extensor surfaces with granular IgA at the dermal papillae are dermatitis herpetiformis.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: Dermatitis herpetiformis is essentially the skin manifestation of which condition?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: Dermatitis herpetiformis is 'coeliac disease of the skin' — the cutaneous manifestation of gluten sensitivity.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: What does the diagnostic direct immunofluorescence show in dermatitis herpetiformis?
options: Linear IgG/C3 at the basement membrane
Granular IgA at the dermal papillae
Linear IgA at the basement membrane
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.answer: Granular IgA at the dermal papillae
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: The gold-standard finding is granular IgA in the dermal papillae on direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: Where are the lesions of dermatitis herpetiformis distributed?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: Dermatitis herpetiformis affects the extensor surfaces symmetrically — elbows, knees, buttocks and scalp.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: What proportion of dermatitis herpetiformis patients have coeliac disease?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: More than 90% of dermatitis herpetiformis patients have coeliac disease, though the gut disease is often silent.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: What is the CORNERSTONE treatment for dermatitis herpetiformis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: A strict lifelong gluten-free diet is the cornerstone — it clears the skin and treats the underlying coeliac disease.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: Which drug gives rapid symptom relief in dermatitis herpetiformis while the diet takes effect?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: Dapsone rapidly relieves the itch/rash within days while the gluten-free diet takes effect (over months).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: What must be checked before starting dapsone in dermatitis herpetiformis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: G6PD must be checked before dapsone because of the risk of haemolysis (also monitor for methaemoglobinaemia and agranulocytosis).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: What is the mechanism of dermatitis herpetiformis?
options: IgA anti-transglutaminase antibodies depositing in the dermal papillae → neutrophilic sub-epidermal blistering
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.answer: IgA anti-transglutaminase antibodies depositing in the dermal papillae → neutrophilic sub-epidermal blistering
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: Gluten sensitivity generates IgA anti-transglutaminase antibodies that deposit in the dermal papillae, recruiting neutrophils and causing sub-epidermal blistering.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: Which HLA types are associated with dermatitis herpetiformis (shared with coeliac)?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: Dermatitis herpetiformis shares the coeliac genetics HLA-DQ2/DQ8.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: Why are intact blisters often hard to find in dermatitis herpetiformis?
options: The intense itch leads to the vesicles being scratched away, leaving excoriations
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.answer: The intense itch leads to the vesicles being scratched away, leaving excoriations
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: The severe itch leads to the vesicles being excoriated, so intact blisters are often hard to find.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: Which coeliac serology is used in the work-up of dermatitis herpetiformis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: Coeliac serology (anti-tTG/anti-endomysial IgA antibodies) is used, with a duodenal biopsy for villous atrophy.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: Why is treating the coeliac disease important even if the gut is 'silent' in dermatitis herpetiformis?
options: They still have the enteropathy and its risks (malabsorption, osteoporosis, lymphoma)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.answer: They still have the enteropathy and its risks (malabsorption, osteoporosis, lymphoma)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: Even with a silent gut, patients still have the coeliac enteropathy and its long-term risks (malabsorption, osteoporosis, lymphoma), which the gluten-free diet reduces.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: Which histological feature is seen in dermatitis herpetiformis?
options: A sub-epidermal blister with neutrophil microabscesses in the dermal papillae
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.answer: A sub-epidermal blister with neutrophil microabscesses in the dermal papillae
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: Histology shows a sub-epidermal blister with neutrophil microabscesses in the dermal papillae.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: Which specialists should co-manage a patient with dermatitis herpetiformis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: Dermatitis herpetiformis should be co-managed with gastroenterology and a dietitian (given the coeliac disease and gluten-free diet), alongside dermatology.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.question: A patient with dermatitis herpetiformis follows a strict gluten-free diet. What effect does it have on the skin?
options: It clears the skin slowly (over months) and treats the coeliac disease
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.answer: It clears the skin slowly (over months) and treats the coeliac disease
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous D.explanation: A strict gluten-free diet clears the skin slowly over months while treating the underlying coeliac disease (dapsone gives rapid relief meanwhile).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.question: A 25-year-old develops discrete, round, smooth bald patches on the scalp with normal underlying skin, and short broken hairs tapering towards the scalp at the patch edges. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.explanation: Discrete round smooth non-scarring bald patches with 'exclamation-mark hairs' are alopecia areata (autoimmune).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.question: What is the master question when assessing any alopecia?
options: Is it male or female pattern?
Is it scarring or non-scarring? (it determines reversibility)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.answer: Is it scarring or non-scarring? (it determines reversibility)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.explanation: Scarring vs non-scarring is the master question — non-scarring preserves the follicle (treatable), scarring destroys it (permanent).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.question: What is the pathognomonic hair finding in alopecia areata?
options: 'Exclamation-mark hairs' (short broken hairs tapering towards the scalp)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.answer: 'Exclamation-mark hairs' (short broken hairs tapering towards the scalp)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.explanation: Exclamation-mark hairs (wider at the top, tapering to the scalp) at the patch edge are pathognomonic of alopecia areata.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.question: Which is the commonest type of alopecia overall?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.explanation: Androgenetic alopecia (male/female pattern) is the commonest type of alopecia.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.question: What drives androgenetic alopecia at the follicle?
options: Androgens (DHT) acting on genetically susceptible follicles → progressive miniaturisation
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.answer: Androgens (DHT) acting on genetically susceptible follicles → progressive miniaturisation
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.explanation: Androgenetic alopecia results from DHT acting on genetically susceptible follicles, causing progressive follicle miniaturisation.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.question: What is the first-line topical treatment for androgenetic alopecia in both men and women?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.explanation: Topical minoxidil is first-line for androgenetic alopecia in both sexes (it prolongs anagen and slows loss/promotes regrowth).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.question: Which oral drug is used for androgenetic alopecia in MEN but is teratogenic and avoided in women of childbearing potential?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.explanation: Finasteride blocks testosterone→DHT and is used in men; it is teratogenic and must be avoided in women of childbearing potential.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.question: A woman with patterned crown thinning also has irregular periods, hirsutism and acne. What should be screened for?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.explanation: Female-pattern hair loss with hyperandrogenic features should prompt screening for PCOS.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.question: A woman notices diffuse hair shedding about 3 months after childbirth, with a positive hair pull test. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.explanation: Diffuse shedding ~3 months after a stressor (e.g. childbirth) with a positive hair pull test is telogen effluvium.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.question: Which alopecia is characterised by loss of follicular openings, scarring and inflammation of the scalp, and is PERMANENT?
options: Scarring (cicatricial) alopecia, e.g. discoid lupus/lichen planopilaris
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.answer: Scarring (cicatricial) alopecia, e.g. discoid lupus/lichen planopilaris
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.explanation: Scarring (cicatricial) alopecia (discoid lupus, lichen planopilaris, folliculitis decalvans) destroys the follicle, causing permanent loss with loss of follicular openings.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.question: Which autoimmune conditions are associated with alopecia areata?
options: Thyroid disease, vitiligo, type 1 diabetes and pernicious anaemia
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.answer: Thyroid disease, vitiligo, type 1 diabetes and pernicious anaemia
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.explanation: Alopecia areata is associated with other autoimmune conditions — thyroid disease, vitiligo, type 1 diabetes, pernicious anaemia (also Down syndrome, atopy).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.question: What is the first-line treatment for localised alopecia areata?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.explanation: Localised alopecia areata is often self-limiting and treated first-line with topical/intralesional corticosteroids.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.question: Which newer class of drug is used for severe alopecia areata?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.explanation: JAK inhibitors (e.g. baricitinib) are a newer treatment for severe alopecia areata.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.question: Alopecia totalis and alopecia universalis describe:
options: The extremes of alopecia areata — totalis = whole scalp; universalis = whole body
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.answer: The extremes of alopecia areata — totalis = whole scalp; universalis = whole body
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.explanation: Alopecia areata can progress to alopecia totalis (whole scalp) and alopecia universalis (whole body).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.question: Which nail change is associated with alopecia areata?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.explanation: Nail pitting and ridging are associated with alopecia areata.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.question: How is telogen effluvium managed?
options: Treat the underlying trigger — it is self-limiting once the trigger resolves
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.answer: Treat the underlying trigger — it is self-limiting once the trigger resolves
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.explanation: Telogen effluvium is self-limiting once the trigger resolves, so management is treating the underlying trigger.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.question: Which scale is used to grade male-pattern androgenetic alopecia?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.explanation: The Norwood-Hamilton scale grades male-pattern (the Ludwig scale grades female-pattern) androgenetic alopecia.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.question: Which anti-androgen options are used for androgenetic alopecia in women, especially with PCOS?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.explanation: Anti-androgens such as spironolactone and the COCP are used in women with androgenetic alopecia, especially with PCOS/hyperandrogenism.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.question: A young adult has smooth, chalk-white, well-demarcated symmetrical patches on the hands and around the mouth, which fluoresce brightly under a Wood's lamp. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.explanation: Smooth, chalk-white, well-demarcated symmetrical patches with bright Wood's-lamp fluorescence are vitiligo (complete depigmentation).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.question: What is the underlying pathophysiology of vitiligo?
options: Autoimmune destruction of melanocytes (loss of pigment cells)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.answer: Autoimmune destruction of melanocytes (loss of pigment cells)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.explanation: Vitiligo is autoimmune destruction/loss of melanocytes, leaving skin with no melanin (depigmentation).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.question: Which phenomenon (new lesions at sites of trauma) is seen in vitiligo?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.explanation: Vitiligo shows the Koebner phenomenon — new lesions developing at sites of skin trauma (shared with psoriasis and lichen planus).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.question: Which autoimmune conditions should be screened for in a patient with vitiligo?
options: Thyroid disease, pernicious anaemia and Addison's disease
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.answer: Thyroid disease, pernicious anaemia and Addison's disease
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.explanation: Vitiligo is associated with thyroid disease, pernicious anaemia and Addison's (± type 1 diabetes, alopecia areata), which should be screened for.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.question: How is vitiligo distinguished from pityriasis versicolor?
options: Vitiligo is complete depigmentation (chalk-white), whereas pityriasis versicolor is hypopigmented, scaly and fungal (Malassezia)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.answer: Vitiligo is complete depigmentation (chalk-white), whereas pityriasis versicolor is hypopigmented, scaly and fungal (Malassezia)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.explanation: Vitiligo is complete depigmentation, whereas pityriasis versicolor is hypopigmented, scaly and caused by Malassezia (fungal).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.question: What does a Wood's lamp demonstrate in vitiligo?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.explanation: Vitiligo patches show bright, sharply-demarcated Wood's-lamp fluorescence, confirming the diagnosis and defining extent (especially in fair skin).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.question: Which is the FIRST-line general measure in managing vitiligo?
options: Sun protection (SPF 50) with vitamin D and cosmetic/psychological support
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.answer: Sun protection (SPF 50) with vitamin D and cosmetic/psychological support
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.explanation: Sun protection (SPF 50), vitamin D and cosmetic/psychological support are first-line general measures, as the depigmented skin lacks photoprotection.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.question: Which topical treatment is particularly useful for facial vitiligo because it does not cause skin atrophy?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.explanation: Topical tacrolimus (a calcineurin inhibitor) is useful for the face in vitiligo because it does not cause skin atrophy.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.question: Which phototherapy is used to repigment vitiligo?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.explanation: Narrowband UVB (TL01) or PUVA phototherapy is used to repigment vitiligo.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.question: Which emerging topical treatment has been approved for non-segmental vitiligo?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.explanation: Ruxolitinib cream, a topical JAK inhibitor, is an emerging treatment approved for non-segmental vitiligo.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.question: Which HLA type is associated with vitiligo?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.explanation: Vitiligo has a genetic predisposition associated with HLA-DR4.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.question: A child has ill-defined pale patches with mild scale on the face following eczema. Which diagnosis is this, rather than vitiligo?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.explanation: Ill-defined pale patches with mild scale in a child, often post-eczema, is pityriasis alba (hypopigmentation), not the complete depigmentation of vitiligo.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.question: Which distribution is typical of vitiligo?
options: Symmetrical involvement of the hands, perioral/periocular skin, feet, elbows and ankles
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.answer: Symmetrical involvement of the hands, perioral/periocular skin, feet, elbows and ankles
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.explanation: Vitiligo typically affects the hands, perioral/periocular skin, feet, elbows and ankles, usually symmetrically (non-segmental).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.question: Which treatment is used to DEPIGMENT the remaining normal skin in extensive refractory vitiligo?
options: A bleaching agent such as monobenzone (monobenzyl ether of hydroquinone)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.answer: A bleaching agent such as monobenzone (monobenzyl ether of hydroquinone)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.explanation: In extensive refractory vitiligo, a bleaching agent (monobenzone/hydroquinone) can depigment the remaining normal skin for a uniform appearance.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.question: Why does vitiligo carry a significant burden despite being medically benign?
options: It has a significant psychological/cosmetic impact
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.answer: It has a significant psychological/cosmetic impact
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.explanation: Vitiligo is medically benign but carries a significant psychological and cosmetic burden, so psychological/cosmetic support is important.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.question: Which segmental vitiligo characteristic is correct?
options: It is dermatomal, occurs in younger patients and is more stable
It always involves the whole body
It is not a form of vitiligo
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.answer: It is dermatomal, occurs in younger patients and is more stable
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Hair & Pigmenta.explanation: Segmental vitiligo is dermatomal, tends to occur in younger patients and is more stable, unlike the common symmetrical non-segmental form.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.question: A young adult develops symmetrical target lesions with a dusky centre, a pale middle ring and a red outer ring on the hands and feet, about 10 days after a cold sore. He is otherwise well. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.answer: Erythema multiforme
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.explanation: Typical 3-ring target lesions on the hands/feet following a cold sore, in a well patient, is erythema multiforme (usually HSV-triggered).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.question: What is the commonest trigger of erythema multiforme?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.answer: Herpes simplex virus (HSV)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.explanation: HSV is by far the commonest trigger of erythema multiforme; recurrent EM is usually HSV-driven.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.question: Describe a TYPICAL target lesion of erythema multiforme.
options: Three concentric zones — a dusky/blistered centre, a pale oedematous middle ring and an erythematous outer ring
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.answer: Three concentric zones — a dusky/blistered centre, a pale oedematous middle ring and an erythematous outer ring
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.explanation: A typical target lesion has three concentric rings: a dusky/blistered centre, a pale oedematous middle and a red outer ring.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.question: Which feature distinguishes erythema multiforme from SJS/TEN?
options: EM has severe mucosal involvement and sheet detachment
EM has typical acral target lesions, is infection (HSV)-triggered and benign, whereas SJS/TEN has dusky detachment, is drug-triggered with severe mucosa and is life-threatening
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.answer: EM has typical acral target lesions, is infection (HSV)-triggered and benign, whereas SJS/TEN has dusky detachment, is drug-triggered with severe mucosa and is life-threatening
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.explanation: EM = typical acral targets, HSV/infection-triggered, benign; SJS/TEN = dusky detachment, truncal, drug-triggered, severe mucosa, deadly (now separate entities).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.question: Where are the lesions of erythema multiforme typically distributed?
options: Acral and symmetrical (hands, feet, extensor limbs, face)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.answer: Acral and symmetrical (hands, feet, extensor limbs, face)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.explanation: Erythema multiforme is acral and symmetrical (hands, feet, extensor limbs, face), spreading centripetally.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.question: Which trigger of erythema multiforme is especially common in children?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.answer: Mycoplasma pneumoniae
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.explanation: Mycoplasma pneumoniae is a common trigger of erythema multiforme in children, sometimes with prominent mucositis.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.question: How is recurrent HSV-driven erythema multiforme best managed?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.answer: Antiviral suppression (e.g. aciclovir/valaciclovir)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.explanation: Recurrent HSV-associated erythema multiforme is managed with long-term antiviral suppression (aciclovir/valaciclovir).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.question: What is the typical natural history of erythema multiforme?
options: Benign and self-limiting, resolving in ~2–4 weeks without scarring
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.answer: Benign and self-limiting, resolving in ~2–4 weeks without scarring
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.explanation: Erythema multiforme is benign and self-limiting, usually resolving in ~2–4 weeks without scarring.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.question: What does an atypical (2-ring) target lesion raise concern for?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.answer: SJS/TEN
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.explanation: Atypical (2-ring) targets, dusky macules and detachment raise concern for SJS/TEN rather than typical erythema multiforme.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.question: What distinguishes EM minor from EM major?
options: Minor is skin only; major has skin + (usually oral) mucosal involvement
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.answer: Minor is skin only; major has skin + (usually oral) mucosal involvement
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.explanation: EM minor is skin only; EM major has additional (usually oral) mucosal involvement, milder than SJS.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.question: How is erythema multiforme diagnosed?
options: Clinically, from typical target lesions and acral distribution (identify the trigger)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.answer: Clinically, from typical target lesions and acral distribution (identify the trigger)
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.explanation: Erythema multiforme is a clinical diagnosis based on typical target lesions and acral distribution; biopsy is reserved for uncertainty.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.question: A patient with erythema multiforme is systemically well with only skin lesions. What is the appropriate management?
options: Supportive care (antihistamines, topical steroids, analgesia) and treat the trigger
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.answer: Supportive care (antihistamines, topical steroids, analgesia) and treat the trigger
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.explanation: EM is self-limiting, so management is supportive with treatment of the underlying trigger; recurrent HSV cases get antiviral suppression.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.question: Erythema multiforme is now regarded as:
options: Part of the same spectrum as SJS/TEN
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.answer: A distinct entity from SJS/TEN
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.explanation: Erythema multiforme is now regarded as a distinct entity from SJS/TEN (a change from older spectrum teaching).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.question: Which is the correct treatment for Mycoplasma-associated erythema multiforme?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.answer: A macrolide or tetracycline
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.explanation: Mycoplasma-associated erythema multiforme is treated with a macrolide or tetracycline (targeting the Mycoplasma).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.question: Which feature argues AGAINST erythema multiforme and towards SJS/TEN?
options: A well patient with acral lesions
Severe mucosal involvement at ≥2 sites with skin detachment and systemic illness
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.answer: A well patient with acral lesions
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.explanation: Severe mucosal involvement, skin detachment and systemic illness point to SJS/TEN rather than benign erythema multiforme.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.question: Which reactive erythema presents with tender red nodules on the shins rather than target lesions?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Erythema Reacti.answer: Erythema nodosum
